entries.ef1182ef2f22771e52049ed05ac5d57580c13dd6: <div sID="gen31043" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="1Cor.3" sID="1Cor.3"/> <div eID="gen31043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31044" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31045" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle, I. Blames the Corinthians for their carnality and divisions, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He instructs them how what was amiss among them might be rectified, by remembering, 1. That their ministers were no more than ministers, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">ver. 5</reference>. 2. That they were unanimous, and carried on the same design, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6-1Cor.3.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. 3. That they built on one and the same foundation, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11-1Cor.3.15">ver. 11-15</reference>. III. He exhorts them to give due honour to their bodies, by keeping them pure (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16-1Cor.3.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>), and to humility and self-diffidence, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18-1Cor.3.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. IV. And dehorts them from glorying in particular ministers, because of the equal interest they had in all, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22-1Cor.3.23">ver. 22 to the end</reference>.
entries.88247eea96fb442a278c28111d9b5123e96ba894: <div eID="gen31045" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31044" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Spirit of Party Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31046" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, <hi type="italic">even</hi> as unto babes in Christ. <hi type="super">2</hi> I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able <hi type="italic">to bear it,</hi> neither yet now are ye able. <hi type="super">3</hi> For ye are yet carnal: for whereas <hi type="italic">there is</hi> among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men? <hi type="super">4</hi> For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> of Apollos; are ye not carnal? <div eID="gen31046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31047" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Paul blames the Corinthians for their weakness and nonproficiency. Those who are sanctified are so only in part: there is still room for growth and increase both in grace and knowledge, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.18">2 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. Those who through divine grace are renewed to a spiritual life may yet in many things be defective. The apostle tells <hi type="italic">them he could not speak to them as unto spiritual</hi> men, <hi type="italic">but as unto carnal</hi> men, <hi type="italic">as to babes in Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">v. 1</reference>. They were so far from forming their maxims and measures upon the ground of divine revelation, and entering into the spirit of the gospel, that is was but too evident they were much under the command of carnal and corrupt affections. They were still mere babes in Christ. They had received some of the first principles of Christianity, but had not grown up to maturity of understanding in them, or of faith and holiness; and yet it is plain, from several passages in this epistle, that the Corinthians were very proud of their wisdom and knowledge. Note, It is but too common for persons of very moderate knowledge and understanding to have a great measure of self-conceit. The apostle assigns their little proficiency in the knowledge of Christianity as a reason why he had communicated no more of the deep things of it to them. They could not bear such food, they needed to be fed with milk, not with meat, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, It is the duty of a faithful minister of Christ to consult the capacities of his hearers and teach them as they can bear. And yet it is natural for babes to grow up to men; and babes in Christ should endeavour to grow in Stature, and become men in Christ. It is expected that their advances in knowledge should be in proportion to their means and opportunities, and their time of professing religion, that they may be able to bear discourses on the mysteries of our religion, and not always rest in plain things. It was a reproach to the Corinthians that they had so long sat under the ministry of Paul and had made no more improvement in Christian knowledge. Note, Christians are utterly to blame who do not endeavour to grow in grace and knowledge. <div eID="gen31047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31048" type="x-p"/> II. He blames them for their carnality, and mentions their contention and discord about their ministers as evidence of it: <hi type="italic">For you are yet carnal; for whereas there are among you envyings, and strifes, and divisions, are you not carnal, and walk as men?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.3">v. 3</reference>. They had mutual emulations, and quarrels, and factions among them, upon the account of their ministers, <hi type="italic">while one said, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">v. 4</reference>. These were proofs of their being carnal, that fleshly interests and affections too much swayed them. Note, Contentions and quarrels about religion are sad evidences of remaining carnality. True religion makes men peaceable and not contentious. Factious spirits act upon human principles, not upon principles of true religion; they are guided by their own pride and passions, and not by the rules of Christianity: <hi type="italic">Do you not walk as men?</hi> Note, It is to be lamented that many who should walk as Christians, that is, above the common rate of men, do indeed walk as men, live and act too much like other men.
entries.abdd39d500a0d81ded3cc6df20b2725abfded71c: <div eID="gen31048" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mutual Agreement of Ministers. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Who then is Paul, and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man? <hi type="super">6</hi> I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. <hi type="super">7</hi> So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. <hi type="super">8</hi> Now he that planteth and he that watereth are one: and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour. <hi type="super">9</hi> For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, <hi type="italic">ye are</hi> God's building. <hi type="super">10</hi> According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise master-builder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. <div eID="gen31049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31050" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle instructs them how to cure this humour, and rectify what was amiss among them upon this head, <div eID="gen31050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31051" type="x-p"/> I. By reminding them that the ministers about whom they contended were but ministers: <hi type="italic">Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom you believed? Even as the Lord gave to every man,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">v. 5</reference>. They are but ministers, mere instruments used by the God of all grace. Some of the factious people in Corinth seem to have made more of them, as if they were lords of their faith, authors of their religion. Note, We should take care not to deify ministers, nor put them into the place of God. Apostles were not the authors of our faith and religion, though they were authorized and qualified to reveal and propagate it. They acted in this office as God gave to every man. Observe, All the gifts and powers that even apostles discovered and exerted in the work of the ministry were from God. They were intended to manifest their mission and doctrine to be divine. It was perfectly wrong, upon their account, to transfer that regard to the apostles which was solely to be paid to the divine authority by which they acted, and to God, from whom they had their authority. <hi type="italic">Paul had planted and Apollos had watered,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Both were useful, one for one purpose, the other for another. Note, God makes use of variety of instruments, and fits them to their several uses and intentions. Paul was fitted for planting work, and Apollos for watering work, but God gave the increase. Note, The success of the ministry must be derived from the divine blessing: <hi type="italic">Neither he that planteth is any thing, nor he that watereth, but God who giveth the increase,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Even apostolical ministers are nothing of themselves, can do nothing with efficacy and success unless God give the increase. Note, The best qualified and most faithful ministers have a just sense of their own insufficiency, and are very desirous that God should have all the glory of their success. Paul and Apollos are nothing at all in their own account, but God is all in all. <div eID="gen31051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31052" type="x-p"/> II. By representing to them the unanimity of Christ's ministers: <hi type="italic">He that planteth and he that watereth are one</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.8">v. 8</reference>), employed by one Master, entrusted with the same revelation, busied in one work, and engaged in one design—in harmony with one another, however they may be set in opposition to each other by factious party-makers. They have their different gifts from one and the same Spirit, for the very same purposes; and they heartily carry on the same design. Planters and waterers are but fellow-labourers in the same work. Note, All the faithful ministers of Christ are one in the great business and intention of their ministry. They may have differences of sentiment in minor things; they may have their debates and contests; but they heartily concur in the great design of honouring God and saving souls, by promoting true Christianity in the world. All such may expect a glorious recompence of their fidelity, and in proportion to it: <hi type="italic">Every man shall receive his own reward, according to his own labour.</hi> Their business is one, but some may mind it more than others: their end or design is one, but some may pursue it more closely than others: their Master also is one, and yet this good and gracious Master may make a difference in the rewards he gives, according to the different service they do: <hi type="italic">Every one's own work shall have its own reward.</hi> Those that work hardest shall fare best. Those that are most faithful shall have the greatest reward; and glorious work it is in which all faithful ministers are employed. <hi type="italic">They are labourers with God,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">synergoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">co-workers, fellow-labourers</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">v. 9</reference>), not indeed in the same order and degree, but in subordination to him, as instruments in his hand. They are engaged in his business. They are working together with God, in promoting the purposes of his glory, and the salvation of precious souls; and he who knows their work will take care they do not labour in vain. Men may neglect and vilify one minister while they cry up another, and have no reason for either: they may condemn when they should commend, and applaud what they should neglect and avoid; but the judgment of God is according to truth. He never rewards but upon just reason, and he ever rewards in proportion to the diligence and faithfulness of his servants. Note, Faithful ministers, when they are ill used by men, should encourage themselves in God. And it is to God, the chief agent and director of the great work of the gospel, to whom those that labour with him should endeavour to approve themselves. They are always under his eye, employed in his husbandry and building; and therefore, to be sure, he will carefully look over them: "<hi type="italic">You are God's husbandry, you are God's building;</hi> and therefore are neither of Paul nor of Apollos; neither belong to one nor the other, but to God: they only plant and water you, but it is the divine blessing on his own husbandry that alone can make it yield fruit. You are not our husbandry, but God's. We work under him, and with him, and for him. It is all for God that we have been doing among you. You are God's husbandry and building." He had employed the former metaphor before, and now he goes on to the other of a building: <hi type="italic">According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise master-builder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon.</hi> Paul here calls himself a wise master-builder, a character doubly reflecting honour on him. It was honourable to be a master-builder in the edifice of God; but it added to his character to be a wise one. Persons may be in an office for which they are not qualified, or not so thoroughly qualified as this expression implies Paul was. But, though he gives himself such a character, it is not to gratify his own pride, but to magnify divine grace. He was a wise master-builder, but the grace of God made him such. Note, It is no crime in a Christian, but much to his commendation, to take notice of the good that is in him, to the praise of divine grace. Spiritual pride is abominable: it is making use of the greatest favours of God to feed our own vanity, and make idols of ourselves. But to take notice of the favours of God to promote our gratitude to him, and to speak of them to his honour (be they of what sort they will), is but a proper expression of the duty and regard we own him. Note, Ministers should not be proud of their gifts or graces; but the better qualified they are for their work, and the more success they have in it, the more thankful should they be to God for his distinguishing goodness: <hi type="italic">I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon.</hi> As before he had said, <hi type="italic">I have planted, Apollos watered.</hi> It was Paul that laid the foundation of a church among them. He had <hi type="italic">begotten them through the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">ch. iv. 15</reference>. Whatever instructors they had besides, <hi type="italic">they had not many fathers.</hi> He would derogate from none that had done service among them, nor would he be robbed of his own honour and respect. Note, Faithful ministers may and ought to have a concern for their own reputation. Their usefulness depends much upon it. <hi type="italic">But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereon.</hi> This is a proper caution; there may be very indifferent building on a good foundation. It is easy to err here; and great care should be used, not only to lay a sure and right foundation, but to erect a regular building upon it. Nothing must be laid upon it but what the foundation will bear, and what is of a piece with it. Gold and dirt must not be mingled together. Note, Ministers of Christ should take great care that they do not build their own fancies or false reasonings on the foundation of divine revelation. What they preach should be the plain doctrine of their Master, or what is perfectly agreeable with it.
entries.129e7dd4947818ad0c748d1ad5a0753e41faa2a4: <div eID="gen31052" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Spiritual Foundation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31053" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; 13 Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. <hi type="super">14</hi> If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. <hi type="super">15</hi> If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. <div eID="gen31053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31054" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle informs us what foundation he had laid at the bottom of all his labours among them—<hi type="italic">even Jesus Christ, the chief corner-stone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Eph. ii. 20</reference>. Upon this foundation all the faithful ministers of Christ build. Upon this rock all the Christians found their hopes. Those that build their hopes of heaven on any other foundation build upon the sand. <hi type="italic">Other foundation can no man lay besides what is laid—even Jesus Christ.</hi> Note, The doctrine of our Saviour and his mediation is the principal doctrine of Christianity. It lies at the bottom, and is the foundation, of all the rest. Leave out this, and you lay waste all our comforts, and leave no foundation for our hopes as sinners. It is in Christ <hi type="italic">only that God is reconciling a sinful world to himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2 Cor. v. 19</reference>. But of those that hold the foundation, and embrace the general doctrine of Christ's being the mediator between God and man, there are two sorts:— <div eID="gen31054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31055" type="x-p"/> I. Some build upon this foundation <hi type="italic">gold, silver, and precious stones</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">v. 12</reference>), namely, those who receive and propagate the pure truths of the gospel, who hold nothing but the <hi type="italic">truth as it is in Jesus,</hi> and preach nothing else. This is building well upon a good foundation, making all of apiece, when ministers not only depend upon Christ as the great prophet of the church, and take him for their guide and infallible teacher, but receive and spread the doctrines he taught, in their purity, with out any corrupt mixtures, without adding or diminishing. <div eID="gen31055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31056" type="x-p"/> II. Others <hi type="italic">build wood, hay, and stubble,</hi> on this foundation; that is, though they adhere to the foundation, they depart from the mind of Christ in many particulars, substitute their own fancies and inventions in the room of his doctrines and institutions, and build upon the good foundation what will not abide the test when the day of trial shall come, and the fire must make it manifest, as wood, hay, and stubble, will not bear the trial by fire, but must be consumed in it. There is a time coming when a discovery will be made of what men have built on this foundation: <hi type="italic">Every man's work shall be made manifest,</hi> shall be laid open to view, to his own view and that of others. Some may, in the simplicity of their hearts, build wood and stubble on the good foundation, and know not, all the while, what they have been doing; but in the day of the Lord their own conduct shall appear to them in its proper light. Every man's work shall be made manifest to himself, and made manifest to others, both those that have been misled by him and those that have escaped his errors. Now we may be mistaken in ourselves and others; but there is a day coming that will cure all our mistakes, and show us ourselves, and show us our actions in the true light, without covering or disguise: <hi type="italic">For the day shall declare it</hi> (that is, every man's work), <hi type="italic">because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13">v. 13</reference>. The day shall declare and make it manifest, the last day, the great day of trial; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">ch. iv. 5</reference>. Though some understand it of the time when the Jewish nation was destroyed and their constitution thereby abolished, when the superstructure which judaizing teachers would have raised on the Christian foundation was manifested to be no better than hay and stubble, that would not bear the trial. The expression carries in it a plain allusion to the refiner's art, in which the fire separates and distinguishes the dross from the gold and silver; as it also will silver and gold and precious stones, that will endure the fire, from wood and hay and stubble, that will be consumed in it. Note, There is a day coming that will as nicely distinguish one man from another, and one man's work from another's, as the fire distinguishes gold from dross, or metal that will bear the fire from other materials that will be consumed in it. In that day, 1. Some men's works will <hi type="italic">abide the trial</hi>—will be found standard. It will appear that they not only held the foundation, but that they built regularly and well upon it—that they laid on proper materials, and in due form and order. The foundation and the superstructure were all of a piece. The foundation-truths, and those that had a manifest connection with them, were taught together. It may not be so easy to discern this connection now, nor know what works will abide the trial then; but that day will make a full discovery. And such a builder shall not, cannot fail of a reward. He will have praise and honour in that day, and eternal recompence after it. Note, Fidelity in the ministers of Christ will meet with a full and ample reward in a future life. Those who spread true and pure religion in all the branches of it, and whose work will abide in the great day, shall receive a reward. And, Lord, how great! how much exceeding their deserts! 2. There are others <hi type="italic">whose works shall be burnt</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">v. 15</reference>), whose corrupt opinions and doctrines, or vain inventions and usages in the worship of God, shall be discovered, disowned, and rejected, in that day—shall be first manifested to be corrupt, and then disapproved of God and rejected. Note, The great day will pluck off all disguises, and make things appear as they are: <hi type="italic">He whose work shall be burnt will suffer loss.</hi> If he have built upon the right foundation wood and hay and stubble, he will suffer loss. His weakness and corruption will be the lessening of his glory, though he may in the general have been an honest and an upright Christian. This part of his work will be lost, turning no way to his advantage, though he himself may be saved. Observe, Those who hold the foundation of Christianity, though they build hay, wood, and stubble, upon it, may be saved. This may help to enlarge our charity. We should not reprobate men for their weakness: for nothing will damn men but wickedness. He shall be saved, <hi type="italic">yet so as by fire,</hi> saved out of the fire. He himself shall be snatched out of that flame which will consume his work. This intimates that it will be difficult for those that corrupt and deprave Christianity to be saved. God will have no mercy on their works, though he may pluck them as brands out of the burning. On this passage of scripture the papists found their doctrine of purgatory, which is certainly hay and stubble: a doctrine never originally fetched from scripture, but invented in barbarous ages, to feed the avarice and ambition of the clergy, at the cost of those who would rather part with their money than their lusts, for the salvation of their souls. It can have no countenance from this text, (1.) Because this is plainly meant of a figurative fire, not of a real one: for what real fire can consume religious rites or doctrines? (2.) Because this fire is to <hi type="italic">try men's works, of what sort they are;</hi> but purgatory-fire is not for trial, not to bring men's actions to the test, but to punish for them. They are supposed to be venial sins, not satisfied for in this life, for which satisfaction must be made by suffering the fire of purgatory. (3.) Because this fire is to <hi type="italic">try every man's works,</hi> those of Paul and Apollos, as well as those of others. Now, no papists will have the front to say apostles must have passed through purgatory fires.
entries.55f3ad3f9db932cefe550bad1dd4802ad000c276: <div eID="gen31056" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Holiness Prescribed. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31057" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? <hi type="super">17</hi> If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which <hi type="italic">temple</hi> ye are. <div eID="gen31057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31058" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle resumes his argument and exhortation, founding it on his former allusion, <hi type="italic">You are God's building,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">v. 9</reference>, and here, <hi type="italic">Know you not that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? If any man defile</hi> (corrupt and destroy) <hi type="italic">the temple of God, him shall God destroy</hi> (the same word is in the original in both clauses); <hi type="italic">for the temple of God is holy, which temple you are.</hi> It looks from other parts of the epistle, where the apostle argues to the very same purport (see <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13-1Cor.6.20">ch. vi. 13-20</reference>), as if the false teachers among the Corinthians were not only loose livers, but taught licentious doctrines, and what was particularly fitted to the taste of this lewd city, on the head of fornication. Such doctrine was not to be reckoned among hay and stubble, which would be consumed while the person who laid them on the foundation escaped the burning; for it tended to corrupt, to pollute, and destroy the church, which was a building erected for God, and consecrated to him, and therefore should be kept pure and holy. Those who spread principles of this sort would provoke God to destroy them. Note, Those who spread loose principles, that have a direct tendency to pollute the church of God, and render it unholy and unclean, are likely to bring destruction on themselves. It may be understood also as an argument against their discord and factious strifes, division being the way to destruction. But what I have been mentioning seems to be the proper meaning of the passage: <hi type="italic">Know you not that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?</hi> It may be understood of the church of Corinth collectively, or of every single believer among them; Christian churches are temples of God. He dwells among them by his Holy Spirit. <hi type="italic">They are built together for a habitation of God through the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">Eph. ii. 22</reference>. Every Christian is a living temple of the living God. God dwelt in the Jewish temple, took possession of it, and resided in it, by that glorious cloud that was the token of his presence with that people. So Christ by his Spirit dwells in all true believers. The temple was devoted and consecrated to God, and set apart from every common to a holy use, to the immediate service of God. So all Christians are separated from common uses, and set apart for God and his service. They are sacred to him—a very good argument this against all fleshly lusts, and all doctrines that give countenance to them. If we are the temples of God, we must do nothing that shall alienate ourselves from him, or corrupt and pollute ourselves, and thereby unfit ourselves for his use; and we must hearken to no doctrine nor doctor that would seduce us to any such practices. Note, Christians are holy by profession, and should be pure and clean both in heart and conversation. We should heartily abhor, and carefully avoid, what will defile God's temple, and prostitute what ought to be sacred to him.
entries.04c4bad59f5ff99ac821d77d6f6e856726a00f8b: <div eID="gen31058" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Humility Prescribed. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31059" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. <hi type="super">19</hi> For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness. <hi type="super">20</hi> And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. <div eID="gen31059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31060" type="x-p"/> Here he prescribes humility, and a modest opinion of themselves, for the remedy of the irregularities in the church of Corinth, the divisions and contests among them: "<hi type="italic">Let no man deceive himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">v. 18</reference>. Do not be led away from the truth and simplicity of the gospel by pretenders to science and eloquence, by a show of deep learning, or a flourish of words, by rabbis, orators, or philosophers." Note, We are in great danger of deceiving ourselves when we have too high an opinion of human wisdom and arts; plain and pure Christianity will be likely to be despised by those who can suit their doctrines to the corrupt taste of their hearers, and set them off with fine language, or support them with a show of deep and strong reasoning. But <hi type="italic">he who seems to be wise must become a fool that he may be wise.</hi> He must be sensible of his own ignorance, and lament it; he must distrust his own understanding, and not lean on it. To have a high opinion of our wisdom is but to flatter ourselves, and self-flattery is the very next step to self-deceit. The way to true wisdom is to sink our opinion of our own to a due level, and be willing to be taught of God. He must become a fool who would be truly and thoroughly wise. The person who resigns his own understanding, that he may follow the instruction of God, is in the way to true and everlasting wisdom. <hi type="italic">The meek will he guide in judgment, the meek will he teach his way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Ps. xxv. 9</reference>. He that has a low opinion of his own knowledge and powers will submit to better information; such a person may be informed and improved by revelation: but the proud man, conceited of his own wisdom and understanding, will undertake to correct even divine wisdom itself, and prefer his own shallow reasonings to the revelations of infallible truth and wisdom. Note, We must abase ourselves before God if we would be either truly wise or good: <hi type="italic">For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">v. 19</reference>. The wisdom which worldly men esteem (policy, philosophy, oratory) <hi type="italic">is foolishness with God.</hi> It is so in a way of comparison with his wisdom. <hi type="italic">He chargeth his angels with folly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job iv. 18</reference>), and much more the wisest among the children of men. <hi type="italic">His understanding is infinite,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.5">Ps. cxlvii. 5</reference>. There can be no more comparison between his wisdom and ours than between his power and being and ours. There is no common measure by which to compare finite and infinite. And much more is the wisdom of man foolishness with God when set in competition with his. How justly does he despise, how easily can he baffle and confound it! <hi type="italic">He taketh the wise in their own craftiness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job v. 13</reference>), he catches them in their own nets, and entangles them in their own snares: he turns their most studies, plausible, and promising schemes against themselves, and ruins them by their own contrivance. Nay, <hi type="italic">He knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.20">v. 20</reference>), that they are vanity, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">Ps. xciv. 11</reference>. Note, God has a perfect knowledge of the thoughts of men, the deepest thoughts of the wisest men, their most secret counsels and purposes: nothing is hidden from him, but <hi type="italic">all things are naked and bare</hi> before him, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 13</reference>. And he knows them to be vanity. The thoughts of the wisest men in the world have a great mixture of vanity, of weakness and folly, in them; and before God their wisest and best thoughts are very vanity, compared, I mean, with his thoughts of things. And should not all this teach us modesty, diffidence in ourselves, and a deference to the wisdom of God, make us thankful for his revelations, and willing to be taught of God, and not be led away by specious pretences to human wisdom and skill, from the simplicity of Christ, or a regard to his heavenly doctrine? Note, He who would be wise indeed must learn of God, and not set his own wisdom up in competition with God's.
entries.682517290334db9b04198d23b806fb7f533d9581: <div eID="gen31060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Against Overvaluing Teachers. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31061" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours; <hi type="super">22</hi> Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; <hi type="super">23</hi> And ye are Christ's; and Christ <hi type="italic">is</hi> God's. <div eID="gen31061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31062" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle founds an exhortation against over-valuing their teachers on what he had just said, and on the consideration that they had an equal interest in all their ministers: <hi type="italic">Therefore let no man glory in men</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">v. 21</reference>)—forget that their ministers are men, or pay that deference to them that is due only to God, set them at the head of parties, have them in immoderate esteem and admiration, and servilely and implicitly follow their directions and submit to their dictates, and especially in contradiction to God and the truths taught by his Holy Spirit. Mankind are very apt to make the mercies of God cross their intentions. The ministry is a very useful and very gracious institution, and faithful ministers are a great blessing to any people; yet the folly and weakness of people may do much mischief by what is in itself a blessing. They may fall into factions, side with particular ministers, and set them at their head, glory in their leaders, and be carried by them they know not whither. The only way to avoid this mischief is to have a modest opinion of ourselves, a due sense of the common weakness of human understanding, and an entire deference to the wisdom of God speaking in his word. Ministers are not to be set up in competition with one another. All faithful ministers are serving one Lord and pursuing one purpose. They were appointed of Christ, for the common benefit of the church: "<hi type="italic">Paul, and Apollos, and Cephas, are all yours.</hi> One is not to be set up against another, but all are to be valued and used for your own spiritual benefit." Upon this occasion also he gives in an inventory of the church's possessions, the spiritual riches of a true believer: "<hi type="italic">All is yours</hi>—ministers of all ranks, ordinary and extraordinary. Nay the world itself is yours." Not that saints are proprietors of the world, but it stands for their sake, they have as much of it as Infinite Wisdom sees to be fit for them, and they have all they have with the divine blessing. "<hi type="italic">Life is yours,</hi> that you may have season and opportunity to prepare for the life of heaven; and <hi type="italic">death is yours,</hi> that you may go to the possession of it. It is the kind messenger that will fetch you to your Father's house. <hi type="italic">Things present</hi> are yours, for your support on the road; <hi type="italic">things to come</hi> are yours, to enrich and regale you for ever at your journey's end." Note, If we belong to Christ, and are true to him, all good belongs to us, and is sure to us. All is ours, time and eternity, earth and heaven, life and death. <hi type="italic">We shall want no good thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Ps. lxxxiv. 11</reference>. But it must be remembered, at the same time, <hi type="italic">that we are Christ's,</hi> the subjects of his kingdom, his property. He is Lord over us, and we must own his dominion, and cheerfully submit to his command and yield themselves to his pleasure, if we would have all things minister to our advantage. All things are ours, upon no other ground than our being Christ's. Out of him we are without just title or claim to any thing that is good. Note, Those that would be safe for time, and happy to eternity, must be Christ's. <hi type="italic">And Christ is God's.</hi> He is the Christ of God, anointed of God, and commissioned by him, to bear the office of a Mediator, and to act therein for the purposes of his glory. Note, All things are the believer's, that Christ might have honour in his great undertaking, and God in all might have the glory. God in Christ reconciling a sinful world to himself, and shedding abroad the riches of his grace on a reconciled world, is the sum and substance of the gospel.  <chapter eID="1Cor.3"/> <div eID="gen31062" type="x-p"/>

entries.1c72a65ca4ecc3355c6add66df1dc346a059134c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16784"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen33053" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:1-23</reference>. Paul Could Not Speak to Them of Deep Spiritual Truths, as They Were Carnal, Contending for Their Several Teachers; These Are Nothing but Workers for God, to Whom They Must Give Account in the Day of Fiery Judgment. The Hearers Are God's Temple, Which They Must Not Defile by Contentions for Teachers, Who, as Well as All Things, Are Theirs, Being Christ's.<div eID="gen33053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16784"/><hi type="bold">1. And I--</hi>that is, as the natural (animal) man cannot receive, so I also could not speak unto you the deep things of God, as I would to the spiritual; but I was compelled to speak to you as I would to MEN OF FLESH. The oldest manuscripts read this for "carnal." The former (literally, "fleshy") implies men wholly of flesh, or natural. Carnal, or fleshly, implies not they were wholly natural or unregenerate (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>), but that they had much of a carnal tendency; for example their divisions. Paul had to speak to them as he would to men wholly natural, inasmuch as they are still carnal (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.3">1Co 3:3</reference>) in many respects, notwithstanding their conversion (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4-1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:4-9</reference>).<div eID="gen33054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">babes--</hi>contrasted with the perfect (fully matured) in Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.5.13">He 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">14</reference>). This implies they were not men wholly of flesh, though carnal in tendencies. They had life in Christ, but it was weak. He blames them for being still in a degree (not altogether, compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">1Co 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>; therefore he says as) babes in Christ, when by this time they ought to have "come unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">Ep 4:13</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">Ro 7:14</reference>, also the oldest manuscripts read, "I am a man of flesh." <div eID="gen33055" type="x-p"/>
entries.b251e75305b69aea79b9e8b6816a41141b56d149: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16785"/><div sID="gen33056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16785"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.12">He 5:12</reference>).<div eID="gen33056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">milk--</hi>the elementary "principles of the doctrine of Christ." <div eID="gen33057" type="x-p"/>
entries.0994e4cadd4d617cac735f271af85c6408a19df4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16786"/><div sID="gen33058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16786"/><hi type="bold">3. envying--</hi>jealousy, rivalry. As this refers to their feelings, "strife" refers to their words, and "divisions" to their actions [Bengel]. There is a gradation, or ascending climax: envying had produced strife, and strife divisions (factious parties) [Grotius]. His language becomes severer now as He proceeds; in <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">1Co 1:11</reference> he had only said "contentions," he now multiplies the words (compare the stronger term, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.6">1Co 4:6</reference>, than in <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>).<div eID="gen33058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carnal--</hi>For "strife" is a "work of the flesh" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.20">Ga 5:20</reference>). The "flesh" includes all feelings that aim not at the glory of God, and the good of our neighbor, but at gratifying self.<div eID="gen33059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walk as men--</hi>as unregenerate men (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.16.23">Mt 16:23</reference>). "After the flesh, not after the Spirit" of God, as becomes you as regenerate by the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">Ro 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.25">Ga 5:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.26">26</reference>). <div eID="gen33060" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4c0ea0ae30e5be3b35d92938c316785693e1709: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16787"/><div sID="gen33061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16787"/>4. (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen33061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are ye not carnal--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Are ye not men?" that is, "walking as men" unregenerate (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.3">1Co 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen33062" type="x-p"/>
entries.274fc7566656150718a28892a662cb8f02e6dcc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16788"/><div sID="gen33063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16788"/><hi type="bold">5. Who then--</hi>Seeing then that ye severally strive so for your favorite teachers, "Who is (of what intrinsic power and dignity) Paul?" If so great an apostle reasons so of himself, how much more does humility, rather than self-seeking, become ordinary ministers!<div eID="gen33063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Paul ... Apollos--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read in the reverse order, "Apollos," &c. Paul." He puts Apollos before himself in humility.<div eID="gen33064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but ministers, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts have no "but." "Who is Apollos ... Paul? (mere) ministers (a lowly word appropriate here, servants), by whom (not "in whom"; by whose ministrations) ye believed."<div eID="gen33065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... Lord gave to every man--</hi>that is, to the several hearers, for it was God that "gave the increase" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen33066" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5a72b0bfdd0945ce9a373ad35230e8e03664f86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16789"/><div sID="gen33067" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16789"/><hi type="bold">6. I ... planted, Apollos watered--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.18.1">Ac 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.1">19:1</reference>). Apollos at his own desire (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.27">Ac 18:27</reference>) was sent by the brethren to Corinth, and there followed up the work which Paul had begun.<div eID="gen33067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God gave the increase--</hi>that is, the growth (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">1Co 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.27">Ac 18:27</reference>). "Believed through grace." Though ministers are nothing, and God all in all, yet God works by instruments, and promises the Holy Spirit in the faithful use of means. This is the dispensation of the Spirit, and ours is the ministry of the Spirit. <div eID="gen33068" type="x-p"/>
entries.fda0c3fb40721e90959e1fb8fd4af2de726aa90f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16790"/><div sID="gen33069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16790"/><hi type="bold">7. neither is he that ... anything ... but God--</hi>namely, is all in all. "God" is emphatically last in the Greek, "He that giveth the increase (namely), God." Here follows a parenthesis, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.8-1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:8-21</reference>, where "Let no man glory in men" stands in antithetic contrast to "God" here. <div eID="gen33069" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a27e028b9e6d7559b6e86193105d56ad6af7af9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16791"/><div sID="gen33070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16791"/><hi type="bold">8. one--</hi>essentially in their aim they are one, engaged in one and the same ministry; therefore they ought not to be made by you the occasion of forming separate parties.<div eID="gen33070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and every man--</hi>rather "but every man." Though in their service or ministry, they are essentially "one," yet every minister is separately responsible in "his own" work, and "shall receive his own (emphatically repeated) reward, according to his own labor." The reward is something over and above personal salvation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">1Co 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">15</reference>; 2Jo 8). He shall be rewarded according to, not his success or the amount of work done, but "according to his own labor." It shall be said to him, "Well done, thou good and (not successful, but) faithful servant, enter thou into the joy of thy Lord" (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.23">Mt 25:23</reference>). <div eID="gen33071" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fe561752d8d7afed8bf12f33fd80ac75dc080d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16792"/><div sID="gen33072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16792"/>9. Translate, as the Greek collocation of words, and the emphasis on "God" thrice repeated, requires, "For (in proof that "each shall receive reward according to his own labor," namely, from God) it is of God that we are the fellow workers (laboring with, but under, and belonging to Him as His servants, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">2Co 5:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">6:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.15.4">Ac 15:4</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.2">1Th 3:2</reference>) of God that ye are the field (or tillage), of God that ye are the building" [Alford]. "Building" is a new image introduced here, as suited better than that of husbandry, to set forth the different kinds of teaching and their results, which he is now about to discuss. "To edify" or "build up" the Church of Christ is similarly used (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.21">Ep 2:21</reference>, 22; 4:29). <div eID="gen33072" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b04e96ad0ed91c6333b189371070d7baefab650: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16793"/><div sID="gen33073" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16793"/><hi type="bold">10. grace ... given unto me--</hi>Paul puts this first, to guard against seeming to want humility, in pronouncing himself "a WISE master builder," in the clause following [Chrysostom]. The "grace" is that "given" to him in common with all Christians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">1Co 3:5</reference>), only proportioned to the work which God had for him to do [Alford].<div eID="gen33073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wise--</hi>that is, skilful. His skill is shown in his laying a foundation. The unskilful builder lays none (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.49">Lu 6:49</reference>). Christ is the foundation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen33074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">another--</hi>who ever comes after me. He does not name Apollos; for he speaks generally of all successors, whoever they be. His warning, "Let every man (every teacher) take heed how," &c., refers to other successors rather than Apollos, who doubtless did not, as they, build wood, hay, &c., on the foundation (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">1Co 4:15</reference>). "I have done my part, let them who follow me see (so the Greek for 'take heed') to theirs" [Bengel].<div eID="gen33075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how--</hi>with what material [Alford]. How far wisely, and in builder-like style (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1Pe 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen33076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buildeth thereupon--</hi>Here the building or superstructure raised on Christ the "foundation," laid by Paul (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">1Co 2:2</reference>) is not, as in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>, 21, the Christian Church made up of believers, the "lively stones" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>), but the doctrinal and practical teaching which the teachers who succeeded Paul, superadded to his first teaching; not that they taught what was false, but their teaching was subtle and speculative reasoning, rather than solid and simple truth. <div eID="gen33077" type="x-p"/>
entries.6aec0417844b76b1890241fc6c4c5d1f48d7e351: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16794"/><div sID="gen33078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16794"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.12">Ac 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen33078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For--</hi>my warning ("take heed," &c. <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">1Co 3:10</reference>) is as to the superstructure ("buildeth thereupon"), not as to the foundation: "For other foundation can no man lay, than that which has (already) been laid (by God) Jesus Christ," the person, not the mere abstract doctrine about Him, though the latter also is included; Jesus, God-Saviour; Christ, Messiah or Anointed.<div eID="gen33079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">can--</hi>A man can not lay any other, since the only one recognized by God has been already laid. <div eID="gen33080" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d58868e11f86ce69d39394ebddcb12152ec18bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16795"/><div sID="gen33081" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16795"/><hi type="bold">12. Now--</hi>rather, "But." The image is that of a building on a solid foundation, and partly composed of durable and precious, partly of perishable, materials. The "gold, silver, precious stones," which all can withstand fire (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.18">Re 21:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.19">19</reference>), are teachings that will stand the fiery test of judgment; "wood, hay, stubble," are those which cannot stand it; not positive heresy, for that would destroy the foundation, but teaching mixed up with human philosophy and Judaism, curious rather than useful. Besides the teachings, the superstructure represents also the persons cemented to the Church by them, the reality of whose conversion, through the teachers' instrumentality, will be tested at the last day. Where there is the least grain of real gold of faith, it shall never be lost (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.12">1Co 4:12</reference>). On the other hand, the lightest straw feeds the fire [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.19">Mt 5:19</reference>). <div eID="gen33081" type="x-p"/>
entries.29ef73d4fe4ce8ed6085cab5cd05e9c55d6de0c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16796"/><div sID="gen33082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16796"/><hi type="bold">13. Every man's work--</hi>each teacher's superstructure on the foundation.<div eID="gen33082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day--</hi>of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">1Co 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.4">1Th 5:4</reference>). The article is emphatic, "The day," that is, the great day of days, the long expected day.<div eID="gen33083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">declare it--</hi>old English for "make it clear" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.4">1Co 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen33084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be revealed by fire--</hi>it, that is, "every man's work." Rather, "He," the Lord, whose day it is (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7">2Th 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>). Translate literally, "is being revealed (the present in the Greek implies the certainty and nearness of the event, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.10">Re 22:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">20</reference>) in fire" (Mal 3:3; 4:1). The fire (probably figurative here, as the gold, hay, &c.) is not purgatory (as Rome teaches, that is, purificatory and punitive), but probatory, not restricted to those dying in "venial sin"; the supposed intermediate class between those entering heaven at once, and those dying in mortal sin who go to hell, but universal, testing the godly and ungodly alike (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2Co 5:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Mark.9.49">Mr 9:49</reference>). This fire is not till the last day, the supposed fire of purgatory begins at death. The fire of Paul is to try the works, the fire of purgatory the persons, of men. Paul's fire causes "loss" to the sufferers; Rome's purgatory, great gain, namely, heaven at last to those purged by it, if only it were true. Thus this passage, quoted by Rome for, is altogether against, purgatory. "It was not this doctrine that gave rise to prayers for the dead; but the practice of praying for the dead [which crept in from the affectionate but mistaken solicitude of survivors] gave rise to the doctrine" [Whately]. <div eID="gen33085" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fac32e331a3f684dbb01205555c1503d16cc7d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16797"/><div sID="gen33086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16797"/><hi type="bold">14. abide--</hi>abide the testing fire (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Mt 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen33086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which he hath built thereupon--</hi>which he built on the foundation.<div eID="gen33087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reward--</hi>wages, as a builder, that is, teacher. His converts built on Christ the foundation, through his faithful teaching, shall be his "crown of rejoicing" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.14">2Co 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.16">Php 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen33088" type="x-p"/>
entries.545e06554d7ee411744405d1ea58eba5646b7551: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16798"/><div sID="gen33089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16798"/><hi type="bold">15. If ... be burnt--</hi>if any teacher's work consist of such materials as the fire will destroy [Alford].<div eID="gen33089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suffer loss--</hi>that is, forfeit the special "reward"; not that he shall lose salvation (which is altogether a free gift, not a "reward" or wages), for he remains still on the foundation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">1Co 3:12</reference>; 2Jo 6).<div eID="gen33090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saved; yet so as by fire--</hi>rather, "so as through fire" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.2">Zec 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.11">Am 4:11</reference>; Jude 23). "Saved, yet not without fire" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.27">Ro 2:27</reference>) [Bengel]. As a builder whose building, not the foundation, is consumed by fire, escapes, but with the loss of his work [Alford]; as the shipwrecked merchant, though he has lost his merchandise, is saved, though having to pass through the waves [Bengel]; Mal 3:1, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">2; 4:1</reference>, give the key to explain the imagery. The "Lord suddenly coming to His temple" in flaming "fire," all the parts of the building which will not stand that fire will be consumed; the builders will escape with personal salvation, but with the loss of their work, through the midst of the conflagration [Alford]. Again, a distinction is recognized between minor and fundamental doctrines (if we regard the superstructure as representing the doctrines superadded to the elementary essentials); a man may err as to the former, and yet be saved, but not so as to the latter (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.15">Php 3:15</reference>). <div eID="gen33091" type="x-p"/>
entries.44af15906d48ac60cc2f06d109b89166204874f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16799"/><div sID="gen33092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16799"/><hi type="bold">16. Know ye not--</hi>It is no new thing I tell you, in calling you "God's building"; ye know and ought to remember, ye are the noblest kind of building, "the temple of God."<div eID="gen33092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye--</hi>all Christians form together one vast temple. The expression is not, "ye are temples," but "ye are the temple" collectively, and "lively stones" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>) individually.<div eID="gen33093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God ... Spirit--</hi>God's indwelling, and that of the Holy Spirit, are one; therefore the Holy Spirit is God. No literal "temple" is recognized by the New Testament in the Christian Church. The only one is the spiritual temple, the whole body of believing worshippers in which the Holy Spirit dwells (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">1Co 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.23">Joh 4:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.24">24</reference>). The synagogue, not the temple, was the model of the Christian house of worship. The temple was the house of sacrifice, rather than of prayer. Prayers in the temple were silent and individual (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.10">Lu 1:10</reference>; 18:10-13), not joint and public, nor with reading of Scripture, as in the synagogue. The temple, as the name means (from a Greek root "to dwell"), was the earthly dwelling-place of God, where alone He put His name. The synagogue (as the name means an assembly) was the place for assembling men. God now too has His earthly temple, not one of wood and stone, but the congregation of believers, the "living stones" on the "spiritual house." Believers are all spiritual priests in it. Jesus Christ, our High Priest, has the only literal priesthood (Mal 1:11; <reference osisRef="Matt.18.20">Mt 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>) [Vitringa]. <div eID="gen33094" type="x-p"/>
entries.b068e900bfe39c83ebbaf826ed54afb187e5ef64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16800"/><div sID="gen33095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16800"/><hi type="bold">17. If any ... defile ... destroy--</hi>rather as the Greek verb is the same in both cases, "destroy ... destroy." God repays in kind by a righteous retaliation. The destroyer shall himself be destroyed. As temporal death was the penalty of marring the material temple (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.2">Le 16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.2">Da 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.30">3, 30</reference>), so eternal death is the penalty of marring the spiritual temple--the Church. The destroyers here (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">17</reference>), are distinct from the unwise or unskilful builders (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">1Co 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">15</reference>); the latter held fast the "foundation" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>), and, therefore, though they lose their work of superstructure and the special reward, yet they are themselves saved; the destroyers, on the contrary, assailed with false teaching the foundation, and so subvert the temple itself, and shall therefore be destroyed. (See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">1Co 3:10</reference>), [Estius and Neander]. I think Paul passes here from the teachers to all the members of the Church, who, by profession, are "priests unto God" (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>). As the Aaronic priests were doomed to die if they violated the old temple (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.43">Ex 28:43</reference>), so any Christian who violates the sanctity of the spiritual temple, shall perish eternally (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.14">He 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.31">31</reference>).<div eID="gen33095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy--</hi>inviolable (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Ha 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen33096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which temple ye are--</hi>rather, "the which (that is, holy) are ye" [Alford], and, therefore, want of holiness on the part of any of you (or, as Estius, "to tamper with the foundation in teaching you") is a violation of the temple, which cannot be let to pass with impunity. Grotius supports English Version. <div eID="gen33097" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8a127639bc1b413cdd29c28707178369eea0346: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16801"/><div sID="gen33098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16801"/><hi type="bold">18. seemeth--</hi>that is, is, and is regarded by himself and others.<div eID="gen33098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wise in this world--</hi>wise in mere worldly wisdom (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1Co 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen33099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let him become a fool--</hi>by receiving the Gospel in its unworldly simplicity, and so becoming a fool in the world's sight [Alford]. Let him no longer think himself wise, but seek the true wisdom from God, bringing his understanding into captivity to the obedience of faith [Estius]. <div eID="gen33100" type="x-p"/>
entries.3de90b07e69f71d83b982f8ea588347e8f2ad9e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16802"/><div sID="gen33101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16802"/><hi type="bold">19. with God--</hi>in the judgment of God.<div eID="gen33101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is written--</hi>in <reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>. The formula of quoting Scripture used here, establishes the canonicity of Job.<div eID="gen33102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He taketh ... wise in ... own craftiness--</hi>proving the "foolishness" of the world's wisdom, since it is made by God the very snare to catch those who think themselves so wise. Literally, "He who taketh ... the whole of the sentence not being quoted, but only the part which suited Paul's purpose. <div eID="gen33103" type="x-p"/>
entries.b43f8e690408f8f9f11301c5375040ee909699ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16803"/><div sID="gen33104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16803"/>20. Quotation from <reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">Psa 94:11</reference>. There it is of men; here it is "of the wise." Paul by inspiration states the class of men whose "thoughts" (or rather, "reasonings," as suits the Greek and the sense of the context) the Spirit designated in the Psalm, "vanity," namely, the "proud" (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.2">Psa 94:2</reference>) and worldly-wise, whom God in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.8">Psa 94:8</reference> calls "fools," though they "boast themselves" of their wisdom in pushing their interests (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.4">Psa 94:4</reference>). <div eID="gen33104" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d73dc22947fb43260787a4934cd7a7ba6d12d2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16804"/><div sID="gen33105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16804"/><hi type="bold">21. let no man glory in men--</hi>resuming the subject from <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">1Co 3:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">31</reference>, where the true object of glorying is stated: "He that glorieth, let him glory in THE Lord." Also <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.6">1Co 4:6</reference>, "That no one of you be puffed up for one against another."<div eID="gen33105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For all things--</hi>not only all men. For you to glory thus in men, is lowering yourselves from your high position as heirs of all things. All men (including your teachers) belong to Christ, and therefore to you, by your union with Him; He makes them and all things work together for your good (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Ro 8:28</reference>). Ye are not for the sake of them, but they for the sake of you (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">2Co 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">15</reference>). They belong to you, not you to them. <div eID="gen33106" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b666ff149956d46070bc954aaba4e859e5557bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16805"/><div sID="gen33107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16805"/>22. Enumeration of some of the "all things." The teachers, in whom they gloried, he puts first (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>). He omits after "Cephas" or Christ (to whom exclusively some at Corinth, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>, professed to belong); but, instead, substitutes "ye are Christ's" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:23</reference>).<div eID="gen33107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">world ... life ... death ... things present ... things to come--</hi>Not only shall they not "separate you from the love of God in Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.39">39</reference>), but they "all are yours," that is, are for you (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Ro 8:28</reference>), and belong to you, as they belong to Christ your Head (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen33108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things present--</hi>"things actually present" [Alford]. <div eID="gen33109" type="x-p"/>
entries.be369052ca4139b905e3ea5370053155523bdd33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16806"/><div sID="gen33110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16806"/><hi type="bold">23. ye are Christ's--</hi>not Paul's, or Apollos,' or Cephas' (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1Co 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.8-Matt.23.10">Mt 23:8-10</reference>). "Neither be ye called masters; for one is your Master, even Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.8">Ro 14:8</reference>). Not merely a particular section of you, but ye all are Christ's (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen33110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ is God's--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1Co 11:3</reference>). God is the ultimate end of all, even of Christ, His co-equal Son (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.28">1Co 15:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.6-Phil.2.11">Php 2:6-11</reference>). <chapter eID="1Cor.3"/>

entries.0a3b26eeb2fbc032f3c0ae684ad3fd4f935993c8: <div eID="gen47360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen47361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen47362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen47362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen47361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen47363" type="x-p"/> Because of the carnal, divided state of the people at Corinth, the apostle was obliged to treat them as children in the knowledge of sacred things, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.3">1Cor 3:1-3</reference>. Some were for setting up Paul, others Apollos, as their sole teachers, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">1Cor 3:4</reference>. The apostle shows that himself and fellow apostles were only instruments which God used to bring them to the knowledge of the truth; and even their sowing, and watering the seed was of no use unless God gave the increase, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5-1Cor.3.8">1Cor 3:5-8</reference>. The Church represented as God's husbandry, and as God's building, the foundation of which is Christ Jesus, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9-1Cor.3.11">1Cor 3:9-11</reference>. Ministers must beware how and what they build on this foundation, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12-1Cor.3.15">1Cor 3:12-15</reference>. The Church of God is his temple, and he that defiles it shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Cor 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1Cor 3:17</reference>. No man should depend on his own wisdom; for the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18-1Cor.3.20">1Cor 3:18-20</reference>. None should glory in man as his teacher; God gives his followers every good, both for time and eternity, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21-1Cor.3.23">1Cor 3:21-23</reference>. <div eID="gen47363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47364" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen47364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47365" type="x-p"/> I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual - This is a continuation of the preceding discourse. See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Cor 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">1Cor 2:15</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.16">1Cor 2:16</reference> (note). <div eID="gen47365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47366" type="x-p"/> But as unto carnal - Σαρκικοις, Persons under the influence of fleshly appetites; coveting and living for the things of this life. <div eID="gen47366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47367" type="x-p"/> Babes in Christ - Just beginning to acquire some notion of the Christian religion, hut as yet very incapable of judging what is most suitable to yourselves, and consequently utterly unqualified to discern between one teacher and another; so that your making the distinctions which you do make, so far from being a proof of mature judgment, is on the contrary a proof that you have no right judgment at all; and this springs from your want of knowledge in Divine things.
entries.da405b077ec88268cf6b1b2f6d6f1f3765bb79f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen47367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47368" type="x-p"/> I have fed you with milk - I have instructed you in the elements of Christianity - in its simplest and easiest truths; because from the low state of your minds in religious knowledge, you were incapable of comprehending the higher truths of the Gospel: and in this state you will still continue. The apostle thus exposes to them the absurdity of their conduct in pretending to judge between preacher and preacher, while they had but a very partial acquaintance even with the first principles of Christianity.
entries.76a92768e2770a75eccaec93549e0ef3355807b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen47368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47369" type="x-p"/> There is among you envying, and strife, and divisions - Ζηλος και ερις και διχοστασιαι. There are three things here worthy of note: these people were wrong in thought, word, and deed. Ζηλος, envying refers to the state of their souls; they had inward grudgings and disaffection towards each other. Ερις, strife or contention, refers to their words; they were continually disputing and contending whose party was the best, each endeavoring to prove that he and his party were alone in the right. Διχοστασιαι, divisions, refers to their conduct; as they could not agree, they contended till they separated from each other, and thus rent the Church of Christ. Thus the envying and grudging led to strife and evil Speaking, and this led to divisions and fixed parties. In this state well might the apostle say, Are ye not carnal, and walk as men? Ye act just as the people of the world, and have no more of the spirit of religion than they.
entries.8a1d5f783bed8a7e93859811a02602a06e5a2e67: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen47369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47370" type="x-p"/> For while one saith, I am of Paul, etc. - It was notorious that both Paul and Apollos held the same creed; between them there was not the slightest difference: when, therefore, the dissentients began to prefer the one to the other, it was the fullest proof of their carnality; because in the doctrines of these apostles there was no difference: so that what the people were captivated by must be something in their outward manner, Apollos being probably more eloquent than Paul. Their preferring one to another on such an account proved that they were carnal - led by their senses and mere outward appearances, without being under the guidance either of reason or grace. There are thousands of such people in the Christian Church to the present day. See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">1Cor 1:10</reference>, etc.
entries.66cade01f2e01df1dcfdcc33ce9d94489f84d7ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen47370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47371" type="x-p"/> Ministers by whom ye believed - The different apostles who have preached unto you the word of life are the means which God has used to bring you to the knowledge of Christ. No one of those has either preached or recommended himself; they all preach and recommend Christ Jesus the Lord. <div eID="gen47371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47372" type="x-p"/> Even as the Lord gave to every man? - Whatever difference there may be in our talents, it is of God's making; and he who knows best what is best for his Church, has distributed both gifts and graces according to his own mind; and, as his judgment is infallible, all these dispensations must be right. Paul, therefore, is as necessary to the perfecting of the Church of Christ as Apollos; and Apollos, as Paul. Both, but with various gifts, point out the same Christ, building on one and the same foundation.
entries.aedfc7bca6a7a22da135517d0fefb55b7ed8e03d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen47372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47373" type="x-p"/> I have planted - I first sowed the seed of the Gospel at Corinth, and in the region of Achaia. <div eID="gen47373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47374" type="x-p"/> Apollos watered - Apollos came after me, and, by his preachings and exhortations, watered the seed which I had sowed; but God gave the increase. The seed has taken root, has sprung up, and borne much fruit; but this was by the especial blessing of God. As in the natural so in the spiritual world; it is by the especial blessing of God that the grain which is sown in the ground brings forth thirty, sixty, or a hundred fold: it is neither the sower nor the waterer that produces this strange and inexplicable multiplication; it is God alone. So it is by the particular agency of the Spirit of God that even good seed, sown in good ground, the purest doctrine conveyed to the honest heart, produces the salvation of the soul.
entries.551b114bd8c209b27e03921787d7f9737b804454: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen47374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47375" type="x-p"/> So then, neither is he that planteth any thing - God alone should have all the glory, as the seed is his, the ground is his, the laborers are his, and the produce all comes from himself.
entries.018ddf146145f3a05646aa4d21198921f29555d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen47375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47376" type="x-p"/> He that planteth and he that watereth are one - Both Paul and Apollos have received the same doctrine, preach the same doctrine, and labor to promote the glory of God in the salvation of your souls. Why should you be divided with respect to Paul and Apollos, while these apostles are intimately One in spirit, design, and operation? <div eID="gen47376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47377" type="x-p"/> According to his own labor - God does not reward his servants according to the success of their labor, because that depends on himself; but he rewards them according to the quantum of faithful labor which they bestow on his work. In this sense none can say, I have labored in vain, and spent my strength for nought.
entries.59485c1197bbf7838df9629a061bd5c463d44228: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen47377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47378" type="x-p"/> For we are laborers together with God - We do nothing of ourselves, nor in reference to ourselves; we labor together in that work which God has given us to do, expect all our success from him, and refer the whole to his glory. It would perhaps be more correct to translate Θεου γαρ εσμεν συνεργοι, we are fellow laborers of God; for, as the preposition συν may express the joint labor of the teachers one with another, and not with God, I had rather, with Bishop Pearce, translate as above: i.e. we labor together in the work of God. Far from being divided among ourselves, we jointly labor, as oxen in the same yoke, to promote the honor of our Master. <div eID="gen47378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47379" type="x-p"/> Ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building - Θεου γεωργιον, Θεου οικοδομη εστε· The word γεωργιον, which we translate husbandry, signifies properly an arable field; so <reference osisRef="Pro.24.30">Pro 24:30</reference> : I went by the Field, γεωργιον, of the slothful; and <reference osisRef="Pro.31.16">Pro 31:16</reference> : The wise woman considereth a Field, γεωργιον, and buyeth it. It would be more literal to translate it, Ye are God's farm: γεωργιον in Greek answers to שדה sadeh in Hebrew, which signifies properly a sown field. <div eID="gen47379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47380" type="x-p"/> Ye are God's building. - Ye are not only the field which God cultivates, but ye are the house which God builds, and in which he intends to dwell.
