7. Neither is he that planteth anything It appears, nevertheless, from what has been already said, that their labor is of some importance. We must observe, therefore, why it is that Paul thus depreciates it; and first of all, it is proper to notice that he is accustomed to speak in two different ways of ministers,
Calvin will be found adverting to the same subject at considerable length, when commenting on 1 Corinthians 9:1. — Ed.
as well as of sacraments. For in some cases he views a minister as one that has been set apart by the Lord for, in the first instance, regenerating souls, and, afterwards, nourishing them up unto eternal life, for remitting sins, (John 20:23,) for renewing the minds of men, for raising up the kingdom of Christ, and destroying that of Satan. Viewed in that aspect he does not merely assign to him the duty of planting and watering, but furnishes him, besides, with the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, that his labor may not be in vain. Thus
“Suyuant ceste consideration;” — “In accordance with this view.”
in another passage he calls himself a minister of the Spirit, and not of the letter, inasmuch as he writes the word of the Lord on men’s hearts. (2 Corinthians 3:6.)
In other cases he views a minister as one that is a servant, not a master — an instrument, not the hand; and in short as man, not God. Viewed in that aspect, he leaves him nothing but his labor, and that, too, dead and powerless, if the Lord does not make it efficacious by his Spirit. The reason is, that when it is simply the ministry that is treated of, we must have an eye not merely to man, but also to God, working in him by the grace of the Spirit — not as though the grace of the Spirit were invariably tied to the word of man, but because Christ puts forth his power in the ministry which he has instituted, in such a manner that it is made evident, that it was not instituted in vain. In this manner he does not take away or diminish anything that belongs to Him, with the view of transferring it to man. For He is not separated from the minister,
“Car en ces facons de parler Christ n’est point separe du ministre;” — “In these modes of expression Christ is not separated (or viewed apart) from the minister.”
but on the contrary His power is declared to be efficacious in the minister. But as we sometimes, in so far as our judgment is depraved, take occasion improperly from this to extol men too highly, we require to distinguish for the purpose of correcting this fault, and we must set the Lord on the one side, and the minister on the other, and then it becomes manifest, how indigent man is in himself, and how utterly devoid of efficacy.
Let it be known by us, therefore, that in this passage ministers are brought into comparison with the Lord, and the reason of this comparison is — that mankind, while estimating grudgingly the grace of God, are too lavish in their commendations of ministers, and in this manner they snatch away what is God’s, with the view of transferring it to themselves. At the same time he always observes a most becoming medium, for when he says, that God giveth the increase, he intimates by this, that the efforts of men themselves are not without success. The case is the same as to the sacraments, as we shall see elsewhere.
Calvin most probably refers here to the statements afterwards made by him, when commenting on Galatians 3:27, to the following effect: “Respondeo, Paulum de Sacramentis bifariam solere loqui. Dum negotium est cum hypocritis, qui nudis signis superbiunt, tum concionatur, quam inanis ac nihili res sit externum signum: et in praeposteram fiduciam fortiter invehitur. Quare? non respicit Dei institutionem, sed impiorum corruptelam. Quum autem fideles alloquitur, qui rite utuntur signis, illa tunc conjungit cum sua veritate, quam figurant. Quare? neque enim fallacem pompam ostentat in Sacramentis, sed quae externa ceremonia figurat, exhibet simul re ipsa. Hinc fit, ut veritas, secundum Dei institutum, conjuncta sit cum signis;” — “I answer, it is customary with Paul to speak of the Sacraments in two different ways. When he has to do with hypocrites, who glory in mere symbols, he in that case proclaims aloud the emptiness and worthlessness of the outward symbol, and denounces in strong terms their absurd confidence. Why so? It is because he has in view, not the ordinance of God, but the corruption of it by wicked men. When, on the other hand, he addresses believers, who make a proper use of the symbols, he in that case views them in connection with the reality which they represent. Why so? It is because he does not make a show of any false splendor as belonging to the Sacraments, but presents before our view in reality what the outward ceremony represents. Hence it comes that, agreeably to the divine appointment, the reality is associated with the symbols.” The same subject is touched upon in the Institutes, volume 3. — Ed.
Hence, although our heavenly Father does not reject our labor in cultivating his field, and does not allow it to be unproductive, yet he will have its success depend exclusively upon his blessing, that he may have the entire praise. Accordingly, if we are desirous to make any progress in laboring, in striving, in pressing forward, let it be known by us, that we will make no progress, unless he prospers our labors, our strivings, and our assiduity, in order that we may commend ourselves, and everything we do to his grace.
entries.76b9f4faf779310066a56249ead119f595b4e5ff: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.8" sID="gen117427" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">He that planteth, and he that watereth are one</hi> He shows farther, from another consideration, that the Corinthians are greatly to blame in abusing, with a view to maintain their own sects and parties, the names of their teachers, who in the meantime are, with united efforts, aiming at one and the same thing, and can by no means be separated, or torn asunder, without at the same time leaving off the duties of their office. <hi type="italic">They are one</hi>, says he; in other words, they are so linked together, that their connection does not allow of any separation, because all ought to have one end in view, and they serve one Lord, and are engaged in the same work. Hence, if they employ themselves faithfully in cultivating the Lord’s field, they will maintain unity; and, by mutual communication, will help each other — so far from their names serving as standards to stir up contendings. Here we have a beautiful passage for exhorting ministers to concord. Meanwhile, however, he indirectly reproves those ambitious teachers, who, by giving occasion for contentions, discovered thereby that they were not the servants of Christ, but the slaves of vain-glory — that they did not employ themselves in <hi type="italic">planting </hi>and <hi type="italic">watering</hi>, but in rooting up and burning.<div eID="gen117428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117429" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Every man will receive his own reward</hi> Here he shows what is the end that all ministers should have in view — not to catch the applause of the multitude, but to please the Lord. This, too, he does with the view of calling to the judgment-seat of God those ambitious teachers, who were intoxicated with the glory of the world, and thought of nothing else; and at the same time admonishing the Corinthians, as to the worthlessness of that empty applause which is drawn forth by elegance of expression and vain ostentation. He at the same time discovers in these words the fearlessness of his conscience, inasmuch as he ventures to look forward to the judgment of God without dismay. For the reason why ambitious men recommend themselves to the esteem of the world is, that they have not learned to devote themselves to God, and that they do not set before their eyes Christ’s heavenly kingdom. Accordingly, as soon as God comes to be seen, that foolish desire of gaining man’s favor disappears.<div eID="gen117429" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117427" osisID="1Cor.3.8" type="section"/>
entries.3733d2de24429e00c36c3cdc8ec323a0e4957702:
9. For we are fellow-laborers with God. Here is the best argument. It is the Lord’s work that we are employed in, and it is to him that we have devoted our labors: hence, as he is faithful and just, he will not disappoint us of our reward. That man, accordingly, is mistaken who looks to men, or depends merely on their remuneration. Here we have an admirable commendation of the ministry — that while God could accomplish the work entirely himself, he calls us, puny mortals,
“Poures vers de terre;” — “Mere worms of the dust.”
to be as it were his coadjutors, and makes use of us as instruments. As to the perversion of this statement by the Papists, for supporting their system of free-will, it is beyond measure silly, for Paul shows here, not what men can effect by their natural powers, but what the Lord accomplishes through means of them by his grace. As to the exposition given by some — that Paul, being God’s workman, was a fellow-workman with his colleagues, that is, with the other teachers — it appears to me harsh and forced, and there is nothing whatever in the case that shuts us up to have recourse to that refinement. For it corresponds admirably with the Apostle’s design to understand him to mean, that, while it is peculiarly the work of God to build his temple, or cultivate his vineyard, he calls forth ministers to be fellow-laborers, by means of whom He alone works; but, at the same time, in such a way, that they in their turn labor in common with him. As to the reward of works, consult my Institutes
The subject of Rewards is largely treated of in the Institutes, volume 2. The reader will find the expression “laborers together with God” commented upon in the Institutes, volume 1. — Ed.
God’s husbandry, God’s building. These expressions may be explained in two ways. They may be taken actively in this sense: “You have been planted in the Lord’s field by the labor of men in such a way, that our heavenly Father himself is the true Husbandman, and the Author of this plantation. You have been built up by men in such a way, that he himself is the true Master-builder.
“Et conducteur de l’oeuvre;” — “And conductor of the work.”
Or, it may be taken in a passive sense, thus: “In laboring to till you, and to sow the word of God among you and water it, we have not done this on our own account, or with a view to advantage to accrue to us, but have devoted our service to the Lord. In our endeavors to build you up, we have not been influenced by a view to our own advantage, but with a view to your being God’s planting and building. This latter interpretation I rather prefer, for I am of opinion, that Paul meant here to express the idea, that true ministers labor not for themselves, but for the Lord. Hence it follows, that the Corinthians were greatly to blame in devoting themselves to men,
“De se rendre suiets aux hommes, et attacher la leurs affections;” — “In making themselves subject to men, and placing their affections there.”
while of right they belonged exclusively to God. And, in the first place, he calls them his husbandry, following out the metaphor previously taken up, and then afterwards, with the view of introducing himself to a larger discussion, he makes use of another metaphor, derived from architecture.
“De la massonerie, ou charpenterie;” — “From masonry, or carpentry.”
1 Corinthians 3:10-15
10. According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
10. Ut saplens architectus, secundum gratiam Dei mihi datam, fundamentum posui, alius autem superaedificat: porro unusquisque videat, quomodo superaedificet.
11. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
11. Fundamentum enim aliud nemo potest ponere, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus.
12. Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble;
12. Si quis autem superstruat super fundamentum hoc aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, ligna, faenum, stipulam,
13. Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is.
13. Cuiuscunque opus manifestum fiet: dies enim manifestabit, quia in igne revelabitur, et cuiuscunque opus quale sit, ignis probabit.
14. If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward.
14. Si cuius opus maneat quod superaedificaverit, mercedem accipiet.
15. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.
15. Si cuius opus arserit, jacturam faciet: ipse autem salvus fiet, sic tamen tanquam per ignem.
“Par feu, ou parmi le feu;” — “By fire, or amidst the fire.”
entries.7c310fb6922e494010943cc3607eda706cc557be: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.10" sID="gen117454" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi><hi type="italic"> As a wise master-builder</hi> It is a most apt similitude, and accordingly it is frequently met with in the Scriptures, as we shall see ere long. Here, however, the Apostle declares his fidelity with great confidence and fearlessness, as it required to be asserted in opposition not merely to the calumnies of the wicked, but also to the pride of the Corinthians, who had already begun to despise his doctrine. The more, therefore, they lowered him, so much the higher does he raise himself up, and speaking as it were from a pulpit of vast height, he declares <note n="171"> <div sID="gen117456" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">I1 leur fait assavoir, et declare fort et ferme</foreign>:” — “He gives them to know, and declares strongly and firmly.”<div eID="gen117456" type="x-p"/> </note> that he had been the first <hi type="italic">master-builder</hi> of God among them in laying the foundation, and that he had with <hi type="italic">wisdom </hi>executed that department of duty, and that it remained that others should go forward in the same manner, regulating the superstructure in conformity with the rule of the foundation. Let us observe that these things are said by Paul <hi type="italic">first </hi>of all for the purpose of commending his doctrine, which he saw was despised by the Corinthians; and, <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, for the purpose of repressing the insolence of others, who from a desire for distinction, affected a new method of teaching. These he accordingly admonishes to attempt nothing rashly in God’s building. Two things he prohibits them from doing: they must not venture to lay another foundation, and they must not raise a superstructure that will not be answerable to the foundation.<div eID="gen117455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117457" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">According to the grace</hi> He always takes diligent heed not to usurp to himself a single particle of the glory that belongs to God, for he refers all thing’s to God, and leaves nothing to himself, except his having been an instrument. While, however, he thus submits himself humbly to God, he indirectly reproves the arrogance of those who thought nothing of throwing <hi type="italic">the grace of God</hi> into the shade, <note n="172"> <div sID="gen117458" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ne faisoyent point de conscience d’amoindrir ou offusquer la grace de Dieu</foreign>;” — “Made no scruple of disparaging or obscuring the grace of God.”<div eID="gen117458" type="x-p"/> </note> provided only they were themselves held in estimation. He hints, too, that there was nothing of the <hi type="italic">grace </hi>of the Spirit in that empty show, for which they were held in esteem, while on the other hand he clears himself from contempt, on the ground of his having been under divine influence. <note n="173"> <div sID="gen117459" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Monstrant, quant a luy qu’il a este pousse et conduit de Dieu, il se defend et maintient contre tout mepris</foreign>;” — “Showing, as to himself, that he had been led on and conducted by God, he guards and defends himself against all contempt.”<div eID="gen117459" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen117457" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117454" osisID="1Cor.3.10" type="section"/>
entries.07b40c51a071e23cbca50bebc21031f055a04bc1: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.11" sID="gen117460" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">For other foundation can no man lay</hi> This statement consists of two parts; <hi type="italic">first</hi>, that Christ is the only foundation of the Church; and <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, that the Corinthians had been rightly founded upon Christ through Paul’s preaching. For it was necessary that they should be brought back to Christ alone, inasmuch as their ears were tickled with a fondness for novelty. It was, too, of no small importance that Paul should be recognized as the principal, and, so to speak, fundamental <hi type="italic">master-builder</hi>, from whose doctrine they could not draw back, without forsaking Christ himself. The sum is this — that the Church must by all means be founded upon Christ alone, and that Paul had executed this department of duty so faithfully that nothing could be found to be wanting in his ministry. Hence, whoever may come after him, can in no other way serve the Lord with a good conscience, or be listened to as ministers of Christ, than by studying to make their doctrine correspond with his, and retain the <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> which he has laid. Hence we infer, that those are not faithful workmen for building up the Church, but on the contrary are <hi type="italic">scatterers </hi>of it, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.30">Matthew 12:30</reference>,) who succeed faithful ministers, but do not make it their aim to conform themselves to their doctrine, and carry forward what has been well commenced, so as to make it quite manifest <note n="174"> <div sID="gen117462" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En sorte qu’on puisse voir a l’oeil</foreign>;” — “So that one may see with the eye.”<div eID="gen117462" type="x-p"/> </note> that they are attempting no new work. For what can be more pernicious than by a new manner of teaching to harass believers, who have been well instructed in pure doctrine, so that they stagger in uncertainty as to the true foundation. Now the fundamental doctrine, which it were unlawful to undermine, is, that we learn Christ, for Christ is the only<hi type="italic"> foundation</hi> of the Church; but there are many who, while they make use of Christ’s name in pretense, tear up the whole truth of God by the roots. <note n="175"> <div sID="gen117463" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Arrachent et renversent entierement</foreign>;” — “They tear up and entirely overthrow”<div eID="gen117463" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen117461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117464" type="x-p"/>Let us observe, then, in what way the Church is rightly built upon Christ. It is when he alone is set forth for righteousness, redemption, sanctification, wisdom, satisfaction and cleansing; in short, for life and glory; or if you would have it stated more briefly, when he is proclaimed in such a manner that his office and influence are understood in accordance with what we found stated in the close of the first chapter. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.30">1 Corinthians 1:30</reference>.) If, on the other hand, Christ is only in some degree acknowledged, and is called a Redeemer only in name, while in the meantime recourse is had to some other quarter for righteousness, sanctification and salvation, he is driven off from the <hi type="italic">foundation</hi>, and spurious <note n="176"> <div sID="gen117465" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et non eonvenantes</foreign>;” — “And not suitable.”<div eID="gen117465" type="x-p"/> </note> stones are substituted in his room. It is in this manner that Papists act, who rob him of almost all his ornaments, leaving him scarcely anything but the bare name. Such persons, then, are far from being founded on Christ. For as Christ is the <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> of the Church, because he is the only source of salvation and eternal life — because in him we come to know God the Father — because in him we have the source of every blessing; if he is not acknowledged as such he is no longer regarded as the <hi type="italic">foundation</hi><div eID="gen117464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117466" type="x-p"/>But it is asked — “Is Christ only a part, or simply the commencement of the doctrine of salvation, as the foundation is merely a part of the building; for if it were so, believers would have only their commencement in Christ, and would be perfected without him. Now this Paul might seem to intimate.” I answer that this is not the meaning of the words; otherwise he would contradict himself when he says elsewhere, that “in him are hid all the treasures of wisdom and <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi>.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.2.3">Colossians 2:3</reference>.) He, then, who has learned Christ, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.20">Ephesians 4:20</reference>,) is already complete in the whole system of heavenly doctrine. But as Paul’s ministry had contemplated rather the founding of the Corinthians than the raising up among them of the top-stone of the building, he merely shows here what he had done in respect of his having preached Christ in purity. With <hi type="italic">respect to </hi>himself therefore, he calls him the <hi type="italic">foundation, </hi>while at the same time he does not thereby exclude him from the rest of the building. In fine, Paul does not put any kind of doctrine in opposition to the knowledge of Christ, but on the contrary there is a comparison between himself and the ministers.<div eID="gen117466" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117460" osisID="1Cor.3.11" type="section"/>
entries.63d06c02b476c2b607bcf1759e3c08f08871e848: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.12" sID="gen117467" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">Now if any man build upon this foundation</hi> He pursues still farther the metaphor. It would not have been enough to have laid the foundation if the entire superstructure did not correspond; for as it were an absurd thing to raise a structure of vile materials on a foundation of gold, so it were greatly criminal to bury Christ under a mass of strange doctrines. <note n="177"> <div sID="gen117469" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce seroit vne chose mal seante que Christ lust suffoque en mettant et meslant auec luy quelques doctrines estranges</foreign>;” — “It were an unseemly thing that Christ should be choked by placing upon him and mixing up with him some strange doctrines.”<div eID="gen117469" type="x-p"/> </note> By<hi type="italic"> gold</hi>, then, and <hi type="italic">silver</hi>, and <hi type="italic">precious stones</hi>, he means doctrine worthy of Christ, and of such a nature as to be a superstructure corresponding to such a foundation. Let us not imagine, however, that this doctrine is apart from Christ, but on the contrary let us understand that we must continue to preach Christ until the very completion of the building. Only we must observe order, so as to begin with general doctrine, and more essential articles, as the foundations, and then go on to admonitions, exhortations, and everything that is requisite for perseverance, confirmation, and advancement.<div eID="gen117468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117470" type="x-p"/>As there is an agreement thus far as to Paul’s meaning, without any controversy, it follows on the other hand, that by <hi type="italic">wood, stubble</hi> and <hi type="italic">hay</hi>, is meant doctrine not answering to the foundation, such as is forged in men’s brain, and is thrust in upon us as though it were the oracles of God. <note n="178"> <div sID="gen117471" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">On vent a force faire receuoir pour oracles et reuelations procedees de Dieu</foreign>;” — “They would force us to receive it as if it were oracles and revelations that have come forth from God.”<div eID="gen117471" type="x-p"/> </note> For God will have his Church trained up by the pure preaching of his own word, not by the contrivances of men, of which sort also is that which has no tendency to edification, as for example curious <hi type="italic">questions</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.4">1 Timothy 1:4</reference>,) which commonly contribute more to ostentation, or some foolish appetite, than to the salvation of men.<div eID="gen117470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117472" type="x-p"/>He forewarns them that <hi type="italic">every man’s work</hi> will one day <hi type="italic">be made manifest of what sort it is</hi>, however it may be for a time concealed, as though he had said: “It may indeed happen, that unprincipled workmen may for a time deceive, so that the world does not perceive how far each one has labored faithfully or fraudulently, but what is now as it were buried in darkness must of necessity come to light, and what is now glorious in the eyes of men, must before the face of God fall down, and be regarded as worthless.”<div eID="gen117472" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117467" osisID="1Cor.3.12" type="section"/>
entries.7d99d406dde074130596cc10c60786ea11d35d61: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.13" sID="gen117473" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">For the day will declare it</hi> In the old translation it is <hi type="italic">the day of the Lord</hi>, <note n="179"> <div sID="gen117475" type="x-p"/> It is so in two of the old English versions. In Wiclif’s version (1380) the rendering is as follows: <hi type="italic">For the dai of the Lord schal declare</hi>. The Rheims version (1582) reads thus: <hi type="italic">For the day of our Lord will declare</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen117475" type="x-p"/> </note> but it is probable that the words <hi type="italic">of the Lord</hi> were added by some one by way of explanation. The meaning unquestionably is complete without that addition. For with propriety we give the name of <hi type="italic">day </hi>to the time when darkness and obscurity are dispelled, and the truth is brought to light. Hence the Apostle forewarns us, that it cannot always remain a secret who have acted fraudulently in the work of the Lord, or who have conducted themselves with fidelity, as though he had said: “The darkness will not always remain: the light will one day break forth; which will make all things manifest.” That day, I own, is God’s — not man’s, but the metaphor is more elegant if you read simply — <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">day</hi>, because Paul in this way conveys the idea, that the Lord’s true servants cannot always be accurately distinguished from false workmen, inasmuch as virtues and vices are concealed by the darkness of the night. That night, however, will not always continue. For ambition is blind — man’s favor is blind — the world’s applause is blind, but this darkness God afterwards dispels in his own time. Take notice, that he always discovers the assurance of a good conscience, and with an unconquerable magnanimity despises perverse judgments; <hi type="italic">first</hi>, in order that he may call back the Corinthians from popular applause to a right rule of judgment; and <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, for the purpose of confirming the authority of his ministry.<div eID="gen117474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117476" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Because it will be revealed by fire.</hi> Paul having spoken of doctrine metaphorically, now also applies metaphorically the name of<hi type="italic"> fire</hi> to the very touchstone of doctrine, that the corresponding parts of the comparison may harmonize with each other. The <hi type="italic">fire</hi>, then, here meant is the Spirit of the Lord, who tries by his touchstone what doctrine resembles <hi type="italic">gold</hi> and what resembles <hi type="italic">stubble</hi> The nearer the doctrine of God is brought to this fire, so much the brighter will be its luster. On the other hand, what has had its origin in man’s head will quickly vanish, <note n="180"> <div sID="gen117477" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Celle, qui aura este forgee au cerveau des hommes s’esuanouira tout incontinent, et s’en ira en fumee</foreign>;” — “That which has been forged in man’s brain, will quickly vanish, and go off in smoke.”<div eID="gen117477" type="x-p"/> </note> as stubble is consumed in the fire. There seems also to be an allusion to <hi type="italic">the day </hi>of which he makes mention: “Not only will those things which vain ambition, like a dark night, concealed among the Corinthians, be brought to light by the brightness of the sun, but there will also be a strength of heat, not merely for drying up and cleansing away the refuse, but also for burning up everything wrong.” For however men may look upon themselves, as forming acute judgments, their discernment, notwithstanding, reaches no farther than appearance, which, for the most part, has no solidity. There is nothing but that <hi type="italic">day </hi>to which the Apostle appeals, that tests everything to the quick, not merely by its brightness, but also by its fiery flame.<div eID="gen117476" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117473" osisID="1Cor.3.13" type="section"/>
entries.26467896f2e7f82264995d5ed791db53668d9191: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.14" sID="gen117478" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> <hi type="italic">If any man’s work remains, he will receive a reward.</hi> His meaning is, that those are fools who depend on man’s estimation, so as to reckon it enough to be approved by men, for <hi type="italic">then only </hi>will the work have praise and recompense — when it has stood the test of the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord</hi> Hence he exhorts His true ministers to have an eye to <hi type="italic">that day.</hi> For by the word <hi type="italic">remains</hi>, he intimates that doctrines fly about as it were in an unsettled state, nay more, like empty bubbles, they glitter for the moment, until they have come to be thoroughly tested. Hence it follows, that we must reckon as nothing all the applauses of the world, the emptiness of which will in a very little be exposed by heaven’s judgment.<div eID="gen117479" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117478" osisID="1Cor.3.14" type="section"/>
entries.75595f00760d69233aa6a6031f86fd70f57fbabc:
15. If any man’s work shall be burned. It is as though he had said: Let no man flatter himself on the ground that, in the opinion of men, he is reckoned among the most eminent master-builders, for as soon as the day breaks in, his whole work must go utterly to nothing, if it is not approved of by the Lord. This, then, is the rule to which every one’s ministry requires to be conformed. Some explain this of doctrine, so that ζημιουσθαι
“Le mot Grec suyuant, qui signifie souffrir perte ou dommage;” — “The Greek word following, which signifies to suffer loss or damage.”
means simply to perish, and then what immediately follows they view as referring to the foundation, because in the Greek θεμελιος (foundation) is in the masculine gender. They do not, however, sufficiently attend to the entire context. For Paul in this passage subjects to trial, not his own doctrine, but that of others.
“Car ce n’est pas sa doctrine, mais celle des autres que Sainct Paul dit, qui viendra a l’examen;” — “For it is not his own doctrine, but that of others, that St. Paul says will come to be tested.”
Hence it were out of place to make mention at present of the foundation. He has stated a little before, that every man’s work will be tried by fire. He comes afterwards to state an alternative, which ought not to be extended beyond that general observation. Now it is certain that Paul spoke there simply of the structure which had been erected upon the foundation. He has already in the first clause promised a reward to good master-builders,
“Et fideles ouuriers;” — “And faithful workmen.”
whose labor shall have been approved of. Hence the contrast in the second clause suits admirably well — that those who have mixed stubble, or wood, or straw, will be disappointed of the commendation which they had expected.
He himself will be saved, etc. It is certain that Paul speaks of those who, while always retaining the foundations, mix hay with gold, stubble with silver, and wood with precious stones — that is, those who build upon Christ, but in consequence of the weakness of the flesh, admit something that is man’s, or through ignorance turn aside to some extent from the strict purity of God’s word. Such were many of the saints, Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and the like. Add to these, if you choose, from those of later times, Gregory and Bernard, and others of that stamp, who, while they had it as their object to build upon Christ, did nevertheless often deviate from the right system of building. Such persons, Paul says, could be saved, but on this condition — if the Lord wiped away their ignorance, and purged them from all dross.
This is the meaning of the clause so as by fire. He means, therefore, to intimate, that he does not take away from them the hope of salvation, provided they willingly submit to the loss of their labor, and are purged by the mercy of God, as gold is refined in the furnace. Farther, although God sometimes purges his own people by afflictions, yet here by the name of fire, I understand the touchstone of the Spirit, by which the Lord corrects and removes the ignorance of his people, by which they were for a time held captive. I am aware, indeed, that, many refer this to the cross,
“Et affliction;” — “And affliction.”
but I am confident that my interpretation will please all that are of sound judgment.
It remains, that we give an answer in passing to the Papists, who endeavor from this passage to prop up Purgatory. “The sinners
“Les pecheurs, (disent-ils);” — “The sinners, (say they).”
whom God forgives, pass through the fire, that they may be saved.” Hence they in this way suffer punishment in the presence of God, so as to afford satisfaction to his justice I pass over their endless fictions in reference to the measure of punishment, and the means of redemption from them, but I ask, who they are that pass through the fire? Paul assuredly speaks of ministers alone. “There is the same reason,” they say, “as to all.” It is not for us
“Je respon, que ce n’est pas a nous;” — “I answer, that it is not for us.”
but for God to judge as to this matter. But even granting them this, how childishly they stumble at the term fire. For to what purpose is this fire,
“Car a quel propos est-il yci parle du feu?” — “For to what purpose does he speak here of fire?”
but for burning up the hay and straw, and on the other hand, for proving the gold and silver. Do they mean to say that doctrines are discerned by the fire of their purgatory? Who has ever learned from that, what difference there is between truth and falsehood? Farther, when will that day come that will shine forth so as to discover every one’s work? Did it begin at the beginning of the world, and will it continue without interruption to the end? If the terms stubble, hay, gold, and silver are figurative, as they must necessarily allow, what correspondence will there be between the different clauses, if there is nothing figurative in the term fire? Away, then, with such silly trifles, which carry their absurdity in their forehead, for the Apostle’s true meaning is, I think, sufficiently manifest.
1 Corinthians 3:16-23
16. Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?
16. An nescitis, quod templum Dei estis et Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis?
17. If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.
17. Si quis ternplum Dei corrumpit,
“Viole destruit;” — “Violates, or destroys.”
hunc perdet Deus. Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos.
18. Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise,
18. Nemo se decipiat, si quis videtur sapiens esse inter vos: in saeculo hoc stultus fiat,
“Si aucvn entre vous cuide estre sage, qu’il soit fait fol en ce monde, afin qu’il soit sage — ou, sage en ce monde, qu’il soit fait fol, afin, etc.;” — “If any one among you seemeth to be wise, let him become a fool in this world, that he may be wise — or, wise in this world, let him become a fool, that,” etc.
ut fiat sapiens.
19. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
19. Sapientia enim mundi huius stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim (Job 5:13) Deprehendens sapientes in astutia sua.
20. And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.
20. Et rursum (Psalm 94:11) Dominus novit cogitationes sapientum vanas esse.
21. Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours;
21. Proinde nemo glorietur in hominibus, omnia enim vestra sunt;
22. Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours;
22. Sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas, sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive prmsentia, sive futura: omnia vestra sunt,
23. And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s.
23. Vos autem Christi; Christus autem Dei.
entries.14d343a37b0dd4d12620bc2c8e620fb1d7d8ca06: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.16" sID="gen117513" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">Know ye not</hi>,<hi type="italic"> etc.</hi> Having admonished the teachers as to their duty, he now addresses himself to the pupils — that they, too, may take heed to themselves. To the teachers he had said, “You are the master-builders of the house of God.” He now says to the people, “You are <hi type="italic">the temples of God.</hi> It is your part, therefore, to take care that you be not, in any way defiled.” Now, the design <note n="190"> <div sID="gen117515" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De cest aduertissement</foreign>;” — “Of this caution.”<div eID="gen117515" type="x-p"/> </note> is, that they may not prostitute themselves to the service of men. He confers upon them distinguished honor in speaking thus, but it is in order that they may be made the more reprehensible; for, as God has set them apart as a <hi type="italic">temple</hi> to himself, he has at the same time appointed them to be guardians of his <hi type="italic">temple</hi> It is sacrilege, then, if they give themselves up to the service of men. He speaks of all of them collectively as being one <hi type="italic">temple of God</hi>; for every believer is a <hi type="italic">living stone</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.5">1 Peter 2:5</reference>,) for the rearing up of the building of God. At the same time they also, in some cases, individually receive the name of <hi type="italic">temples</hi> We shall find him a little afterwards (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.19">1 Corinthians 6:19</reference>) repeating the same sentiment, but for another purpose. For in that passage he treats of chastity; but here, on the other hand, he exhorts them to have their faith resting on the obedience of Christ alone. The interrogation gives additional emphasis; for he indirectly intimates, that he speaks to them of a thing that they knew, while he appeals to them as witnesses.<div eID="gen117514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117516" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And the Spirit of God.</hi> Here we have the reason why they are <hi type="italic">the temple of God</hi> Hence <hi type="italic">and </hi>must be understood as meaning <hi type="italic">because</hi> <note n="191"> <div sID="gen117517" type="x-p"/> Audieras, <hi type="italic">et </hi>fama fitit. Virg. Eclog. 9. 11.<div eID="gen117517" type="x-p"/> </note> This is customary, as in the words of the poet — “Thou hadst heard it, <hi type="italic">and </hi>it had been reported.” “For this reason,” says he, “are ye the <hi type="italic">temples of God</hi>, because He dwells in you by his Spirit; for no unclean place can be the habitation of God.” In this passage we have an explicit testimony for maintaining the divinity of the Holy Spirit. For if he were a creature, or merely a gift, he would not make us <hi type="italic">temples of God</hi>, by dwelling in us. At the same time we learn, in what manner God communicates himself to us, and by what tie we are bound to him — when he pours down upon us the influence of his Spirit.<div eID="gen117516" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117513" osisID="1Cor.3.16" type="section"/>
entries.44bb2f6561390d38056e725d671f4be415edce3e: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.17" sID="gen117518" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">If any man corrupts the temple of God.</hi> He subjoins a dreadful threatening — that, as the <hi type="italic">temple of God</hi> ought to be inviolably sacred, that man, whoever he may be, that corrupts it, will not pass with impunity. The kind of profanation of which he now speaks, is, when men intrude themselves, so as to bear rule in the Church in the place of God. For as that faith, which is devoted to the pure doctrine of Christ, is called elsewhere spiritual <hi type="italic">chastity</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11.2">2 Corinthians 11:2</reference>,) so it also sanctifies our souls for the right and pure worship of God. For as soon as we are tinctured with the contrivances of men, the temple of God is polluted, as it were, with filth, because the sacrifice of faith, which he claims for himself alone, is in that case offered to creatures.<div eID="gen117519" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117518" osisID="1Cor.3.17" type="section"/>
entries.cf53d5b8ffcfb0ce203eebc1f7760c9b0a3d55ec: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.18" sID="gen117520" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> <hi type="italic">Let no man deceive himself</hi> Here he puts his finger upon the true sore, as the whole mischief originated in this — that they were wise in their own conceit. Hence he exhorts them not to deceive themselves with a false impression, by arrogating any wisdom to themselves — by which he means, that all are under a mistake, who depend upon their own judgment. Now, he addresses himself, in my opinion, to hearers as well as teachers. For the former discovered a partiality for those ambitious men, and lent an ear to them, <note n="192"> <div sID="gen117522" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Trop facilement</foreign>;” — “Too readily.”<div eID="gen117522" type="x-p"/> </note> because they had too fastidious a taste, so that the simplicity of the gospel was insipid to their taste; while the latter aimed at nothing but show, that they might be in some estimation. He accordingly admonishes both to this effect — “Let no one rest satisfied with his own wisdom, but let him <hi type="italic">who thinketh himself to be wise, become a fool in this world</hi>,” or, “<hi type="italic">Let </hi>him who is distinguished in this world by reputation for wisdom, of his own accord empty himself, <note n="193"> <div sID="gen117523" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Soit fait fol en soy de son bon gre s’abbaissant, et s’aneantissant soymesme</foreign>;” — “Let him become, of his own accord, a fool in his own estimation, abasing and emptying himself.”<div eID="gen117523" type="x-p"/> </note> and <hi type="italic">become a fool</hi> in his own estimation.”<div eID="gen117521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117524" type="x-p"/>Farther, in these words the Apostle does not require, that we should altogether renounce the wisdom that is implanted in us by nature, or acquired by long practice; but simply, that we subject it to the service of God, so as to have no wisdom but through his word. For this is what is meant by <hi type="italic">becoming a fool in this world</hi>, or in our own estimation — when we are prepared to give way to God, and embrace with fear and reverence everything that he teaches us, rather than follow what may appear to us plausible. <note n="194"> <div sID="gen117525" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Bon et raisonnable</foreign>;” — “Good and reasonable.”<div eID="gen117525" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen117524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117526" type="x-p"/>The meaning of the clause <hi type="italic">in this world</hi>, is as though he had said — “According to the judgment or opinion of the world.” For the wisdom of the world is this — if we reckon ourselves sufficient of ourselves for <hi type="italic">taking counsel </hi>as to all matters (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.13.2">Psalm 13:2</reference>) for governing ourselves, and for managing whatever we have to do — if we have no dependence on any other <note n="195"> <div sID="gen117527" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que de nous-mesmes</foreign>;” — “Than ourselves.”<div eID="gen117527" type="x-p"/> </note> — if we feel no need of the guidance of another, but are <hi type="italic">competent </hi>to govern ourselves. <note n="196"> <div sID="gen117528" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Nous semble que nous sommes assez suffisans de nous conduire, et gouuerner nous-mesmes</foreign>;” — “It appears to us, that we are quite competent to conduct and govern ourselves.”<div eID="gen117528" type="x-p"/> </note> He, therefore, on, the other hand, is <hi type="italic">a fool in this world</hi>, who, renouncing his own understanding, allows himself to be directed by the Lord, as if with his eyes shut — who, distrusting himself, leans wholly upon the Lord, places his whole wisdom in him, and yields himself up to God in docility and submission. It is necessary that our wisdom should in this way vanish, in order that the will of God may have authority over us, and that we be emptied of our own understanding, that we may be filled with the wisdom of God. At the same time, the clause <note n="197"> <div sID="gen117529" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">En ce monde</hi></foreign>;” — “<hi type="italic">In this world</hi>.”<div eID="gen117529" type="x-p"/> </note> may either be taken in connection with the first part of the verse, or joined with the last, but as the meaning is not much different, I leave every one to choose for himself.<div eID="gen117526" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117520" osisID="1Cor.3.18" type="section"/>
entries.eeb32d3b0ebc20ad91bf093def1b64b845ee767c: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.19" sID="gen117530" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">For the wisdom of this world</hi> This is an argument taken from things opposite. To maintain the one is to overturn the other. As, therefore, <hi type="italic">the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God</hi>, it follows that we cannot be wise in the sight of God, unless we are fools in the view of the world. We have already explained (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.20">1 Corinthians 1:20</reference>) what he means by <hi type="italic">the wisdom of this world</hi>; for natural perspicacity is a gift of God, and the liberal arts, and all the sciences by which wisdom is acquired, are gifts of God. They are confined, however, within their own limits; for into God’s heavenly kingdom they cannot penetrate. Hence they must occupy the place of handmaid, not of mistress: nay more, they must be looked upon as empty and worthless, until they have become entirely subject to the word and Spirit of God. If, on the other hand, they set themselves in opposition to Christ, they must be looked upon as dangerous pests, and, if they strive to accomplish anything of themselves, as the worst of all hindrances. <note n="198"> <div sID="gen117532" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce sont de grans empeschemens, et bien a craindre</foreign>;” — “They are great hindrances, and much to be dreaded.”<div eID="gen117532" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence <hi type="italic">the wisdom of the world</hi>, in Paul’s acceptation, is that which assumes to itself authority, and does not allow itself to be regulated by the word of God, or to be subdued, so as to yield itself up in entire subjection to him. Until, therefore, matters have come to this, that the individual acknowledges that he knows nothing but what he has learned from God, and, giving up his own understanding; resigns himself unreservedly to Christ’s guidance, he is wise in the world’s account, but he is foolish in the estimation of God.<div eID="gen117531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117533" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For it is written, He taketh the wise</hi> He confirms this from <hi type="italic">two </hi>Scripture proofs, the <hi type="italic">first </hi>of which is taken from <reference osisRef="Bible:Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>, where the wisdom of God is extolled on this ground, that no wisdom of the world can stand before it.<div eID="gen117533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117534" type="x-p"/>Now it is certain, that the Prophet speaks there of those that are cunning and crafty; but as the wisdom of man is invariably such without God, <note n="199"> <div sID="gen117535" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quand la sagesse de Dieu n’y est point</foreign>;” — “When the wisdom of God is not in it.”<div eID="gen117535" type="x-p"/> </note> it is with good reason that Paul applies it in this sense, — that whatever wisdom men have of themselves is reckoned of no account in the sight of God. The <hi type="italic">second </hi>is from <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.94.11">Psalm 94:11</reference>, where David, after claiming for God alone the office and authority of the Instructor of all, adds, that <hi type="italic">He knows the thoughts of all to be vain.</hi> Hence, in whatever estimation they are held by us, they are, in the judgment of God, <hi type="italic">vain</hi> Here we have an admirable passage for bringing down the confidence of the flesh, while God from on high declares that everything that the mind of man conceives and contrives is mere <hi type="italic">vanity</hi> <note n="200"> <div sID="gen117536" type="x-p"/> “The humbling tendency ef the statement referred to is well brought out by Fuller of Kettering. (<hi type="italic">Fuller</hi>’<hi type="italic">s Works</hi>, volume 4, p. 89.)<div eID="gen117536" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen117534" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117530" osisID="1Cor.3.19" type="section"/>
entries.0e561e7bad2347c41419c1e9bcd834f995247f1e: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.21" sID="gen117537" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore let no man glory in men</hi> As there is nothing that is more <hi type="italic">vain </hi>than man, how little security there is in leaning upon an evanescent shadow! Hence he infers with propriety from the preceding statement, that we must not <hi type="italic">glory in men</hi>, inasmuch as the Lord thus takes away from mankind universally every ground of glorying. At the same time this inference depends on the whole of the foregoing doctrine, as will appear ere long. For as we belong to Christ alone, it is with good reason that he teaches us, that any supremacy of man, by which the glory of Christ is impaired, involves sacrilege.<div eID="gen117538" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117537" osisID="1Cor.3.21" type="section"/>
entries.ecdd0963f3a1054123ca273eabef2edfdefbd3d7: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.3.22" sID="gen117539" type="section"/> <div sID="gen117540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">All things are yours.</hi> He proceeds to show what place and station teachers should occupy <note n="201"> <div sID="gen117541" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est a dire, quelle estime on en doit auoir</foreign>;” — “That is to easy, in what esteem they ought to be held.”<div eID="gen117541" type="x-p"/> </note> — such as not to detract in any degree from the authority of Christ, the one Master. As therefore Christ is the Church’s sole master, and as he alone without exception is worthy to be listened to, it is necessary to distinguish between him and others, as even Christ himself has testified respecting himself, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.8">Matthew 23:8</reference>,) and no other is recommended to us by the Father with this honorable declaration, <note n="202"> <div sID="gen117542" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Nul autre ne nous a este donne du Pere authorize de ce titre et commandement</foreign>;” — “No other has been given to us by the Father, authorized by this distinction and injunction.”<div eID="gen117542" type="x-p"/> </note> “Hear ye him.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.17.5">Matthew 17:5</reference>.) As, therefore, he alone is endowed with authority to rule us by his word, Paul says that others <hi type="italic">are ours</hi> — meaning, that they are appointed to us by God with the view of our making use of them — not that they should exercise dominion over our consciences. Thus on the one hand, he shows that they are not useless, and, on the other hand, he keeps them in their own place, that they may not exalt themselves in opposition to Christ. What he adds, as to <hi type="italic">death</hi>,<hi type="italic"> life</hi>, and the rest, is hyperbolical, so far as concerns the passage before us. He had it in view, however, to reason, as it were, from the greater to the less, in this manner. “Christ having put in subjection to us <hi type="italic">life</hi> and <hi type="italic">death</hi>, and everything, can we doubt, whether he has not also made men subject to us, to help us by their ministrations — not to oppress us by tyranny.”<div eID="gen117540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen117543" type="x-p"/>Now if any one takes occasion from this to allege, that the writings both of Paul and of Peter are subject to our scrutiny, inasmuch as they were men, and are not exempted from the common lot of others, I answer, that Paul, while he does not by any means spare himself or Peter, admonishes the Corinthians to distinguish between the person of the individual, and the dignity or distinction of office. “As for myself, viewed as a man, I wish to be judged of simply as a man, that Christ alone may have distinction in our ministry.” This, however, in a general way, we must hold, <note n="203"> <div sID="gen117544" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour vne maxime</foreign>;” — “As a maxim.”<div eID="gen117544" type="x-p"/> </note> that all who discharge the office of the ministry, are <hi type="italic">ours</hi>, from the highest to the lowest, so that we are at liberty to withhold our assent to their doctrine, until they show that it is from Christ. For they must all be <hi type="italic">tried</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.4.1">1 John 4:1</reference>,)and we must yield obedience to them, only when they have satisfactorily shown themselves to be faithful servants of Christ. Now as to Peter and Paul, this point being beyond all controversy, and the Lord having furnished us with amply sufficient evidence, that their doctrine has come forth from Him, when we receive as an oracle from heaven, and venerate everything that they have delivered to us, we hear not so much <hi type="italic">them</hi>, as Christ speaking in them.<div eID="gen117543" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.3.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen117539" osisID="1Cor.3.22" type="section"/>

Christ is God’s This subjection relates to Christ’s humanity, for by taking upon him our flesh, he assumed “the form” and condition “of a servant,” that he might make himself obedient to his Father in all things. (Philippians 2:7, 8.) And assuredly, that we may cleave to God through him, it is necessary that he have God as his head (1 Corinthians 11:3.) We must observe, however, with what intention Paul has added this. For he admonishes us, that the sum of our felicity consists in this,
“Car il nous donne a entendre, et remonstre, que le comble et la perfection de nostre felicite consiste la;” — “For he gives us to understand, and shows, that the summit and perfection of our felicity consists in this.”
that we are united to God who is the chief good, and this is accomplished when we are gathered together under the head that our heavenly Father has set over us. In the same sense Christ said to his disciples,
“Ye ought to rejoice, because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I,” (John 14:28,)
for there he set himself forth as the medium, through which believers come to the original source of every blessing. It is certain, that those are left destitute of that signal blessing, who depart from the unity of the Head.
“Qui ne retienent ce seul Chef;” — “Who do not retain that sole Head.”
Hence this order of things suits the connection of the passage — that those subject themselves to Christ alone, who desire to remain under God’s jurisdiction.

imo nec me ipsum diiudico.

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:438" />10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.5. & 12.3.</ns0:note> According to the grace of God which is given unto me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">

                     </ns0:gap> here signifies either the ability which God hath gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> to preach the Gospel, or the Apostolical Office, to which God had called him, he maketh both to proceed from God, and to be the effects of his free love and favour to him.</ns0:note>, as a wise master-builder I have laid <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 21.24.</ns0:note> the foundation <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">According to this he saith, Look as wise Master-builder first layeth the foundation, then buildeth upon the foundation which he hath laid. So he being the first, whom God pleased to im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ploy in this his work at <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> had laid the foundation, that is, had first preached the Gospel in this famous City: thus the first preaching of the Gospel is called, a laying the founda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.20. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.1.</ns0:note>, and another buildeth there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Afterwards <ns0:hi>Apollos</ns0:hi> and other Ministers further carried on that work of preaching the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel amongst them.</ns0:note>. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 4.11.</ns0:note> But let every man take heed how he build<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth thereupon <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">But (saith he) whoever cometh to preach after me, had need take heed what he buildeth; for, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.8. <ns0:hi>Though we or an Angel from heaven preach any other Gospel unto you, then that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.</ns0:hi>

               <ns0:p n="11">11 For other foundation can no man lay, then <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 28.16. Matt. 16.18.</ns0:note> that is laid, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 2.20.</ns0:note> which is Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Can</ns0:hi> in this Text doth not signifie a meer natural power, but a rightful power; no man by any just right or authority can lay any other foundation, can preach any other Doctrine of Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation, than that which I have already preached, which is the Doctrine of Salvation by Jesus Christ. <ns0:hi>Neither is there salvation in any other; for there is no other Name under heaven given amongst men whereby we must be saved,</ns0:hi> Acts 4.12.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Now if any man build upon this foundation, gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Apostle is discoursing <ns0:hi>metaphorically,</ns0:hi> he had compared the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> to a building, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. and called them there <ns0:hi>Gods building:</ns0:hi> they were built upon the Doctrine of the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel, the <ns0:hi>Doctrine of the Apostles</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> who had preached Christ to them, this was the foundation, and had told us, that none, by any pretence of right, could lay any other foundation. But there was to be a superstructure upon this foundation, which might be of various materials, he names six; three very good and excellent, <ns0:hi>gold, silver,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>precious stones</ns0:hi>; three others vile and invaluable, <ns0:hi>wood, hay, stubble.</ns0:hi> By these he either means <ns0:hi>good</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>bad works,</ns0:hi> or rather <ns0:hi>good</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>bad Doctrines. Good Doctrine</ns0:hi> is signified by the <ns0:hi>gold, silver,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>precious stones</ns0:hi> men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned. <ns0:hi>Bad Doctrine</ns0:hi> by the <ns0:hi>wood, hay,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>stubble</ns0:hi> mentioned; by which may be understood various degrees of bad Doctrine, as some Doctrines are more pernicious and damnable than o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers, though the other also be false, unprofitable, trivial, and of no significancy to the good of Souls, but had, as they are un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />profitable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.5.</ns0:note> Every mans work shall be made mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fest <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Now, saith he, there will come a time when every man's, that is, every <ns0:hi>Teacher's</ns0:hi> work or Doctrine, shall be made mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fest. As the metal is brought to the touch-stone to be tryed, whether it be <ns0:hi>gold</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>silver,</ns0:hi> or some baser metal; so there will come a time, when all Doctrines shall be tryed and made ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifest, whether they be of God or no.</ns0:note>: for the day shall declare it <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">What day shall de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clare it is not so steadily agreed by Interpreters. Some by <ns0:hi>a day</ns0:hi> here understand a long time, in process of time it shall be de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clared, as indeed <ns0:hi>erroneous Doctrines</ns0:hi> have not used to obtain or prevail long. <ns0:hi>Dagon</ns0:hi> falls before the Ark. Others understand it of a <ns0:hi>day of adversity</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>great affliction,</ns0:hi> the day of Gods vengeance; and indeed thus it is often seen, a false faith or a lye believed, will not carry a man through the difficulties which he meeteth with in an evil day: the Truths of the Gospel are of that nature, that they will give a Soul relief and support in a day of affliction, and under Gods severest dispensations, but errors and falshoods will not do it. Others understand by <ns0:hi>the day</ns0:hi> here mentioned the day of Judgment, which is indeed of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten called <ns0:hi>the day of the Lord, Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.8. and described by fire, <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 2.3. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.18. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.10. but this Text saith not, <ns0:hi>The day of the Lord,</ns0:hi> but only <ns0:hi>the day.</ns0:hi> It seemeth there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore rather to signifie the bright shining out of the Gospel: for the Text seemeth to speak of such a manifestation as shall be in this life, not in the day of Judgment. The same thing is also to be understood.</ns0:note>, because <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 1.7. & 4.12.</ns0:note> it <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>is reveal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> shall be revealed by fire, and the fire shall try eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry mans work of what sort it is <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>fire</ns0:hi> here mentioned, not the fire of Gods wrath, or the fire of affliction and adversity, nor the fire of the last Judgment, but the truth of the Gospel shi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning forth in the World, and burning up the dross and stubble of corrupt false Doctrine, that shall bring all the Doctrines which men teach, to the tryal.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 If any mans work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">If any Preacher keeps the foundation, and the Doctrine which he hath built upon the true foundation, prove consonant to the will of Christ, God will reward him for his labour. He shall hear the voice saying, <ns0:hi>Well done, good and faithful servant, enter thou into thy masters joy.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 If any mans work shall be burnt, he shall suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fer loss <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">But if his <ns0:hi>work do not abide,</ns0:hi> if he shall appear upon the more clear and bright shining out of the truth of the Gospel, that though he hath held the foundation right, yet he hath built upon it <ns0:hi>wood, hay,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>stubble,</ns0:hi> mixed <ns0:hi>fables</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>idle sto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries,</ns0:hi> and corrupt Doctrine with the Doctrine of the Gospel, he shall suffer <ns0:hi>loss by it,</ns0:hi> either by afflicting hand of God, or by a loss of his reputation, or some other way.</ns0:note>: but he himself shall be saved: yet so, as by fire <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">But yet God will not cast off a Soul for every such errour, if he keeps to the main foundation Jesus Christ. <ns0:hi>He shall be saved,</ns0:hi> though it be as by <ns0:hi>fire,</ns0:hi> that is, with difficulty, which certainly is a more natural sense of this Text, than those give, who interpret <ns0:hi>as by fire,</ns0:hi> of the fire of the Gospel, or the fire of <ns0:hi>Purgatory,</ns0:hi> of which the Papists understand it. For. 1. It is, and always hath been a <ns0:hi>proverbial</ns0:hi> form of speech to express a thing ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tained by difficulty, we say, <ns0:hi>It is got out of the fire,</ns0:hi> &c. 2. For the fire of <ns0:hi>Purgatory,</ns0:hi> it is a fiction and meer imaginary thing, and of no further significancy, than to make the <ns0:hi>Popes</ns0:hi> Chimney smoak. 3. Heb. 3.6.</ns0:note> ye are the temple of God? and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Apostle, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. had called the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> and the particular Members of it, <ns0:hi>Gods building,</ns0:hi> after this he had inlarged in a discourse concerning the builders, and the foundation and superstructure upon that foundation, now he returns again to speak of the whole Church, whom he here calleth the <ns0:hi>Temple of God,</ns0:hi> with a manifest allusion to that noble and splendid House which <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> first builded, and was afterwards rebuild<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by <ns0:hi>Zorobabel, Ezra,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nehemiah</ns0:hi> at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> as the pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lick place for the Jewish Church to meet in to worship God according to the prescript of the <ns0:hi>Levitical Law,</ns0:hi> in which House God was said to <ns0:hi>dwell,</ns0:hi> because there he met his people, and blessed them, and there he gave answers to them from the Mercy-seat: he calls them the <ns0:hi>Temple of God,</ns0:hi> because they were <ns0:hi>built,</ns0:hi> that is, effectually called for this very end, that they might be <ns0:hi>to the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved, Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.6. And as the Apostle <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> further expoundeth this Text, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.5. <ns0:hi>The people of God are a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual sacrifices acceptable to God by Iesus Christ.</ns0:hi> And God by his <ns0:hi>Spirit dwelt in them,</ns0:hi> both by his person, and by his gifts and graces, which is a far more noble dwelling in them, than the dwelling of God was in the Jewish Temple. From this Text may be fetch'd an evident proof of the Divine Nature, of the third Person in the blessed Trinity; for he is not only called here the Spirit of God, but he is said to <ns0:hi>dwell in the Saints:</ns0:hi> which dwelling of God in his people, is that very thing which maketh them the <ns0:hi>Temple of God</ns0:hi>; and those who are here called, <ns0:hi>The Temple of God,</ns0:hi> are <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.19. called, <ns0:hi>The Temple of the Holy Ghost.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 If any man <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>destroy.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The word which we translate <ns0:hi>defile</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>destroy</ns0:hi> (for the <ns0:hi>Greek word</ns0:hi> is the same for both) signifieth to <ns0:hi>violate, corrupt,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>destroy.</ns0:hi> Our Translators generally render it <ns0:hi>corrupt, Chap.</ns0:hi> 15.33. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.2. & 11.3. Eph. 4.22. <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 19.2. The people of God which are here called, <ns0:hi>The Temple of God</ns0:hi> are defiled, either by imbibing false Doctrine, or being tempted to any loosness of life and conversation. Now (saith the Apostle) if any one goeth about to do this, which all Preachers do, who teach any false Doctrine, or any Principles that lead to a liberty for the flesh, or lead an ill and scandalous life, God shall destroy those men.</ns0:note>: for the temple of God is ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">For as the Temple of God of old was a place builded and set apart for holy uses, and therefore not without great peril to be abused and profaned: so those that are the people of God, are by God called and set apart in a more im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediate eminent manner for the honour and glory of God, and therefore cannot de debauched or defiled by any as instruments in that action, without exceeding great peril and hazard to them that endeavour and attempt any such thing.</ns0:note>, which <ns0:hi>temple</ns0:hi> ye are.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:438" />18 <ns0:note place="margin">Prov. 3.7. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 5.21.</ns0:note> Let no man deceive himself: <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">There are some that with their <ns0:hi>Eloquence,</ns0:hi> and flourishes of words, or with their philosophical notions and reasonings (which, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.8. the Apostle calls <ns0:hi>vain deceit</ns0:hi>) or with their <ns0:hi>Traditions</ns0:hi> after the rudiments of the World (as the Apostle addeth in that place) would cheat and deceive your Souls, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der a pretence of making you wonderfully wise: the wisdom of the World is foolishness with God.</ns0:note> if any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">If any of you seemeth unto others, or seemeth unto himself, that is, thinketh that he is endued with what the World calleth Wisdom.</ns0:note>, let him become a fool, that he may be wise <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">If ever he would be truly wise, wise unto God, and to eternal Life and Salvation, let him be contented by the wise men and <ns0:hi>Philoso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phers</ns0:hi> of this World to be lookt upon as a fool, and let him be willing to deny himself in any notions or opinions of his, which he hath taken up upon the credit of his natural Reason and philosophical Principles, which agree not with the Divine Reve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation, that so he may be truly and spiritually wise, truly under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing, savouring, and believing what God hath in his Word revealed, and is alone able to make the man of God wise to Salvation, throughly furnished unto every good work.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">God accounteth that folly, which the World calleth wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, and indeed it is so (for God cannot err, nor be mistaken in his judgment) the <ns0:hi>Philosophers</ns0:hi> and wise men of the World propose the happiness of man as their end, which indeed is the true end which all men aim at, and do propound to themselves, true wisdom directeth the best means in order to the best end. Whatsoever directeth not to the best end, or to what is not the best mean in order to that end, is not wisdom, but real folly; <ns0:hi>worldly wisdom</ns0:hi> neither directeth to the best end, for it looks at no further happiness than that of this life, nor yet to the <ns0:hi>best means,</ns0:hi> and therefore is truly what God accounts it, foolish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:note>: for it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">And to see the wise and learned men of the World thus <ns0:hi>err</ns0:hi> both in their judgment and practice, is no wonder at all; for God is set out of old by <ns0:hi>Eliphaz,</ns0:hi> as one that <ns0:hi>taketh the wise in their own craftiness, Iob</ns0:hi> 5.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And againe, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">And again it was said by the Psalmist, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 94.11. <ns0:hi>That the Lord knoweth that the thoughts of man are vanity:</ns0:hi> mans coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sels, imaginations, reasonings, they are all vanity; they propose to themselves ends which they cannot attain, and pursue them by means that are inefficacious with reference to their ends.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Therefore let no man glory in men <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Seeing therefore that Christ is but one, his Ministers but one, and no more than Ministers, by whom you believed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. and the principal efficiency of any saving work begun, or car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ried on in your Souls to any degree of perfection, is from God, and the Ministers work in that effect nothing, compared with his, seeing you are Gods husbandry, Gods building, not meer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly mans, and the <ns0:hi>Temple of God,</ns0:hi> not mens Temple, leave your glorying in men, and saying, I am of <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> or I am of <ns0:hi>Apollos,</ns0:hi> glory only in this, that you are Christ's: besides,</ns0:note>: for all things are yours <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">why do you glory in a particular Minister when all is yours, as if two joynt-heirs in an Estate should glory in this or that particular house or inclosure, when the whole Estate is joyntly theirs, all theirs.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come, all are yours.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:gap>. 11.3.</ns0:note> ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> Christs, and Christ <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Gods <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Here are in these two verses three things asserted: 1. <ns0:hi>The Believers Title to all things.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>The specialty of their Title.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>The force of the Apostles argument from hence, why they should not glory in men.</ns0:hi> He had said before, <ns0:hi>All things are yours,</ns0:hi> which he re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peats again, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. They have a right and title to all things, and all things are for their good, use, and advantage. A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst these he first reckons <ns0:hi>Ministers.</ns0:hi> Every one of them might lay a claim to <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Apollos,</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi>; for they were all Servants of Christ for the use of his Church, a part of which they were, then he goes on, and saith, <ns0:hi>the world,</ns0:hi> that is, the things of the world are theirs, that is, whatsoever portion of them the Providence of God orderly disposed to them, they had a true title to it, and it was for their use and advantage; so were the lives and deaths of Gods Ministers, their own lives and deaths, all things present, and all things that were to come, they were all theirs by a just title: if the Providence of God gave them to them in an orderly way, they might comfortably use them. They themselves were Christ's, they were not of <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> nor of <ns0:hi>Apollos,</ns0:hi> nor of <ns0:hi>Peter.</ns0:hi> He that had the Bride was the Bridegroom, these Ministers were but the friends of their Bridegroom: and <ns0:hi>Christ is Gods,</ns0:hi> the Son of God by an eternal Generation, the Servant of God as man, and born under the Law, so yielding obedience to his Father, the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> or a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nointed, and <ns0:hi>sent of God</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Mediator.</ns0:hi> All things are Gods, by God given to Christ, by Christ given to, and sanctified for you, that makes the Believers <ns0:hi>special title to all things.</ns0:hi> The men of the world derive their title to what they have, from God alone, as Creator, they derive not from Christ, as being ingrafted and implanted into him. Hence the Apostle rightly concludes their vanity, in glorying in their Relation to this or that spe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cial Apostle or Minister, whenas they had a true and just right to the labours of all Ministers, and ought to look upon all faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Ministers, as Gods gifts to his whole Church, and for the advantage and benefit of all: yet his hindreth not, but that people ought to have their particular <ns0:hi>Pastors</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Teachers,</ns0:hi> to whom they ought ordinarily to attend in their Ministry; but they ought not to have their persons in such admiration, as for them to despise or slight any other faithful Ministers, nor to make Parties and Factions in the Church of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
